#3466. What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s new limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that company’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

“The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” says Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan says that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.

CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION

Not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.

In episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

“One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that showed that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”

As for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”

Real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch plan: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the company’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.

CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF

True. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.

CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF

I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, said Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”

#3465. The Naruto Movie Sounds Like It Could Be Better Than We Ever Imagined

Fresh off making the best "Spider-Man" movie in about a decade with "Brand New Day," director Destin Daniel Cretton is plunging into the Land of Fire and ninjas, adapting Masashi Kishimoto's manga/worldwide phenomenon "Naruto" into a live-action film, two years after it was first announced. Translating a battle shonen manga/anime into live-action carries negative associations of past, failed attempts. Why bother moving a story designed to stretch reality's limits to a medium that's inherently more confining than a hand-drawn one? Will "Naruto" break this curse? It has a huge stage to do so, and the early steps look promising.

Deadline has reported that actor Hiroyuki Sanada ("Shogun," "John Wick: Chapter 4") is in negotiations to star in "Naruto" as Hiruzen Sarutobi, the Third Hokage and leader of Naruto's ninja village, Konohagakure. Sanada is the second major actor rumored to be joining "Naruto," after reports in August that Charles Melton had been approached to play Kakashi Hatake, Naruto's masked sensei.

This alone suggests "Naruto" is serious about getting impressive talent: one of the coolest actors alive in Sanada, and a major young actor in Melton, who's won acclaim for his performances in "May December" and "Beef" Season 2. Not for nothing, Sanada and Melton are Japanese and Korean American, respectively — no whitewashing here, so far, contrary to "Naruto" fans' long-standing jokes about Tom Holland or Timothée Chalamet starring as Naruto.

"Naruto" has launched a "global" search/audition process for the movie's three young leads: Naruto and his teammates Sasuke Uchiha and Sakura Haruno. That suggests the film's creators are looking for young actors — possibly, even plausibly, unknowns — who can embody those characters first without prioritizing pre-existing star power.

Casting Hiroyuki Sanada as the Third Hokage suggests the "Naruto" team is already looking to the horizon and seeing sequels. Hiruzen is only a background part of the first "Naruto" arc, "The Land of Waves" (which is the ideal starting place for a movie series). But he takes center stage in the second and third arcs, where one of his former students, the snake-like Orochimaru, serves as the main villain. Hiruzen gets a major action sequence confronting Orochimaru, and casting Sanada — a martial artist who holds a black belt in karate, just as Charles Melton has one in taekwondo — seems like casting with that scene in mind.

If the goal is adapting the "Naruto" manga as a whole, then forward thinking will be key. The manga runs 700 chapters, divided into several story arcs; you'd likely need somewhere between seven and 10 movies to complete it. The live-action "Naruto" is being produced by studio Lionsgate in partnership with Sony. Lionsgate recently proved once more that "The Hunger Games" is a reliable hit for them with the success of "Sunrise on the Reaping." But it's never smart to put all your eggs in one basket. "Naruto" hits overlapping demographic appeal and even some similar story beats as "The Hunger Games" (like children becoming killers and the tragic horrors of war).

Moreover, comic books have become the prime IP of Hollywood these past two decades, and yet manga outsells American comics many times over. Manga/anime is in the cultural mainstream for anyone younger than a young millennial, and the first studio to crack that could be sitting on a cultural gold mine. So, yeah, Lionsgate has a strong incentive to get "Naruto" right, and the talent it's recruiting suggests they understand that.

Even if Destin Daniel Cretton doesn't stick around for any of those potential "Naruto" sequels (I have to imagine Sony and Marvel Studios want him back for more "Spider-Man" movies), getting him as director for the first is another sign that Lionsgate is taking this seriously. Look at what he's directed, and consider how he's intent on casting actors with genuine martial arts bona fides for "Naruto," and it's clear why he's the man for the job.

An essential part of "Naruto" is its fight choreography, which is more choreographed around hand-to-hand martial arts than most other battle shonen. Yes, the ninjas in "Naruto" use "jutsus," or magical/superpowered attacks powered by spiritual energy, or chakra. But the core of the series' fight scenes is mano-a-mano fights that lay on the brutality and raw emotion; that's especially true in Naruto and Sasuke's various duels.

The combat in "Naruto" likewise employs parkour acrobatics in the vein of wuxia. (In-universe, ninja learn to channel their chakra to balance on, climb, and run through trees.) Cretton directing "Shang-Chi," a wuxia-flavored Marvel movie, and Spider-Man, who webslings through New York City like how Naruto and his ilk dash through forests, gives him the perfect experience to deliver the heightened-but-not-completely intensity of the action from the early "Naruto" arcs.

Cretton also has the perfect sensei to consult with in Masashi Kishimoto, who has endorsed Cretton as the perfect director for the project, the same way that "One Piece" creator Eiichiro Oda personally approved elements of Netflix's "One Piece" series. "One Piece" proved live-action shonen manga/anime can work in the TV format, and "Naruto" might be the project that proves it can be a blockbuster movie.

Anthony Mackie seems to have figured out how to get through an Avengers: Doomsday interview without giving Marvel's security team a heart attack. Whenever someone asks him about the upcoming Marvel movie, he just starts playing with the title. It was funny the first time. Now that he's doing it again, I'm beginning to think the MCU's Captain America has found his new catchphrase.

Considering the last couple of weeks Mackie has had, I can't blame him. The actor recently found himself explaining a comment about Paul Bettany that sent Marvel fans into spoiler-detective mode. In a new interview with Entertainment Tonight, Mackie was asked how the news of Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch returning would affect the Avengers. It's a fair question, and he offered an answer that sounded pretty ominous, even if it didn't exactly tell us what happens:

Well, it’s like, remember you saw ‘X-Men’ and like, Jean Grey, like, blew up the whole planet? Imagine that, but on a different planet. That’s what it’s giving me.

I don't know that Jean Grey actually destroyed an entire planet in the Fox X-Men movies, but I appreciate the former Falcon’s commitment to making the comparison sound terrifying. And considering Wanda's history in WandaVision and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, I understand why he'd reach for another famously powerful mutant. What he doesn't explain is how Sam Wilson and the other Avengers plan to deal with any of it.

The interviewer followed up by asking if he was really claiming he had no idea about Wanda's return. That's when Mackie delivered the line I've now decided needs to be printed on a shirt:

I had no idea. It’s a lot of Doom in a day… That’s it. That’s my line. It’s a lot of Doom in a day. I mean, I came up with that. I feel like that’s bars.

This is becoming a pattern. Mackie essentially gave the same answer to gave Josh Horowitz on Happy Sad Confused, describing the movie as a day full of a lot of, shall we say, fucking Doom. Now he's refined the joke into a cleaner line he can use in just about any interview. I hope he keeps going.

His caution makes sense after the Bettany episode. Mackie previously mentioned seeing the Vision actor while filming, which fueled speculation about an unannounced Doomsday appearance. He later defended his comments on The Tonight Show, as he explained that Bettany had been working on VisionQuest nearby. Of course, that didn't stop fans from analyzing every word. Take a look at this recent interview:

Anthony Mackie weighs in on Scarlet Witch’s surprise return in ‘VisionQuest’ and what it could mean for ‘Avengers: Doomsday.’ 👀 https://t.co/LVZo6kteX6November 23, 2026

I love watching Anthony Mackie navigate all this. With Robert Downey Jr. returning to Marvel as Doctor Doom and so many heroes converging for the next Avengers movie, fans have plenty of questions. Mackie has apparently decided the title will answer most of them.

Avengers: Doomsday hits the 2026 movie schedule on Dec. 18. Until then, I'm waiting to see how many more ways Mackie can fit the word "Doom" into a sentence before somebody at Marvel takes his microphone away.

#3463. 87 Years Later, Dorothy's Best Wizard Of Oz Line Remains The Greatest Movie Quote Ever

What's the most famous film in history? "Star Wars"? "Citizen Kane"? "Casablanca"? Victor Fleming's "The Wizard of Oz" has to be in contention. "Oz" remains as beloved almost a century after its premiere as it was in its day, and everything of note about the movie is embedded into pop culture, from the Yellow Brick Road to the characters who walk it to the Flying Monkeys. Ever since the 1950s, the film has become a staple of television programming, ensuring generations that came long after the movie itself still learn from an early age to cherish it.

Margaret Hamilton as The Wicked Witch of the West is the definitive cultural image of a wicked witch. Her green skin, black outfit with a pointed hat, and, of course, her broom are the blueprint for countless other witches (not to mention, Halloween costumes).

"Oz" wasn't the first ever color film, despite misconceptions otherwise, but it still represents a turning point. One reason the error sticks is how well it maps onto the movie's narrative. Dorothy Gale's (Judy Garland) story begins in plain old Kansas, shot in black and white. Then, when she lands in Oz, the movie turns into technicolor. Even today, the film's rainbow-colored fantasy remains a beautiful spectacle.

Many, many unofficial "Wizard of Oz" sequels and prequels have been made, including various animated movies and TV series. Later "Oz" movies range from the (surprisingly frightening) 1985 sequel "Return to Oz" to Sam Raimi's 2013 prequel about the wizard, "Oz the Great and Powerful." Then of course, there's the stage musical (and now two-part movie) "Wicked," the only "Oz"-inspired work that even comes close to the original movie's cultural status.

As you almost certainly know, during "The Wizard of Oz," Dorothy and her little dog Toto get swept away by  a twister to the Land of Oz. After a grand adventure, she realizes the power to go home was with her all along in the ruby slippers gifted to her by Glinda the Good Witch (Billie Burke). So, calling on the slippers' power, Dorothy closes her eyes and wakes up in her bed back in Kansas after affirming "There's no place like home!" (suggesting, unlike in its source material, Dorothy's adventure was all a dream). She then declares to her Aunt Em (Clara Blandick) and everyone else present that there is, indeed, no place like home.

At the beginning of "The Wizard of Oz," Dorothy wants to see more of the world beyond Kansas, as she sings in "Somewhere Over The Rainbow." She finally runs away to save her dog Toto from the cruel Mrs. Gulch (Margaret Hamilton), but then rushes back when traveling performer Professor Marvel (Frank Morgan) warns her that her aunt, uncle, and friends back at the farm worry for her.

In 2014, Skyler Gisondo joined the Night at the Museum franchise to play Ben Stiller’s son, Nick Daley. While he’d worked a lot as a kid before that, this role marked a turning point in his career. Now, he’s reteaming with Stiller for Focker In-Law on the 2026 movie schedule, and he’s playing his son…again. So, considering that, I asked the Superman actor how his first time playing Stiller’s kid impacted his work in the Meet the Parents franchise, and he told me why it was a very full-circle experience.

As a Meet the Parents and Night at the Museum fan, I couldn’t get enough of this reunion. It was also fun to see Stiller and Gisondo reunite now, because I’ve become such a big fan of the work the Booksmart actor did between Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb and Focker In-Law. So, I asked Gisondo how his history with Stiller played into this experience on Focker In-Law; he said:

It was great. I mean, Night at the Museum was such a formative experience for me. I was 17. It was my first time being a bigger part of a bigger movie like that. And Ben really took me under his wing then, and was so good to me. And I think I had almost forgotten how much I took from that time.

Again, while Skyler Gisondo was a successful child actor, Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb (which you can watch with a Disney+ subscription) was a turning point for him. It makes sense that he learned a lot from Stiller on it that has impacted his career since.

Speaking of his career, after Night at the Museum, Gisondo booked roles in projects like Vacation, Santa Clarita Diet, Booksmart and more. Also, his last couple of years leading up to his reunion with Stiller have been fantastic. He played the beloved Jimmy Olsen in James Gunn’s Superman, he finished the final season of The Righteous Gemstones, and he was a standout alongside Robert Pattinson in Primetime. Truly, he has become quite the actor, and he’s one of my favorite rising stars.

So, to hear that Stiller impacted him is really sweet. What makes it even sweeter is that while working on Focker In-Law, Gisondo realized all this as he started to notice that some of the things he does as an actor are things Stiller does too:

And then getting reunited on this, like 12 years later, there was all these things I would notice Ben doing before takes or something, and realize that I've done that my whole adult life. And I kind of had forgotten where I’d gotten it from or something. And I think it was really helpful for this movie to have that kind of built-in familial sort of relationship.

Knowing about Stiller and Gisondo’s history certainly played into my enjoyment of the movie, especially since the last time I saw them together, Gisondo was a kid. Now, he’s all grown up, and that fact certainly plays into Focker In-Law.

To that point, in Focker In-Law, we follow Greg Focker (Stiller) as he reunites with his family, including his son Henry (Gisondo). Things get chaotic because Henry brings home his girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande), and he plans to propose to her. After that, we dive into a lot of chaos as Greg butts heads with Henry’s partner, and obviously it leads to some very funny familial hijinks. It’s silly, and it was such a fun way to see the Night at the Museum actors work together again all these years later.

Without the knowledge of their history, their dynamic is funny in Focker In-Law. However, knowing this is the second time they’ve played father and son, and also knowing that Gisondo really had a full-circle moment realizing how much Stiller has impacted him, makes it even better.

So, if you’d like to see this Night at the Museum reunion, and if you’d like to try and clock the ways in which Stiller and Gisondo are similar as actors, you can catch Focker In-Law in theaters on November 25.

#3460. Is Star Trek: The Animated Series Canon? It's Complicated

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Even to this day, there's a debate over whether or not "Star Trek: The Animated Series" counts as a canonical installment in the "Star Trek" franchise. The show ran for 22 episodes over the course of two seasons from 1973 to 1974, and, in certain respects, it's actually better than "The Original Series." Being an animated 30-minute show, it's a lot more efficient in its storytelling and is able to visually realize far more expansive and outlandish ideas. For instance, it features aliens that evolved from plants and an episode that takes place largely underwater.

That said, there are aspects of "The Animated Series" that directly contradict other entries in the franchise. Take "The Counter-Clock Incident," an episode that introduces Commodore Robert April (James Doohan) as an elderly white man. However, when the character reappeared on "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," he was played by Adrian Holmes, a Black actor. Then there's the episode "The Magicks of Megas-Tu," which is about the USS Enterprise traveling to the center of the galaxy and encountering a being believed to be the Devil. The thing is, this clashes with the film "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier," in which the Enterprise's crew meets an entity thought to be God at the center of the galaxy.

According to the oral history book "The Fifty-Year Mission," edited by Mark Altman and Edward Gross, "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry himself even said that "The Animated Series" isn't strictly canon. Yet, a lot of the show has become canon over time, as some of the people who worked on it discussed in the short documentary "Drawn to the Final Frontier" (itself included on the series' DVD release).

It should immediately be pointed out that "Star Trek: The Animated Series" was penned by many of the same writers who worked on "Star Trek: The Original Series," was created by Gene Roddenberry, and features most of the actors from "The Original Series" to boot (save for Walter Koenig as Chekov). What's more, in "Drawn to the Final Frontier," longtime "Trek" writer D.C. Fontana noted that "The Animated Series" had a research company to ensure it aligned with the events of "The Original Series." As she put it, "It has to follow. It has to make sense. They have to agree."

Expanding on this, "The Magicks of Megas-Tu" writer Larry Brody addressed the canon question directly in "Drawn to the Final Frontier," stating, "My take as to whether this fits into the 'Star Trek' legacy is that it fits into my version of the 'Star Trek' legacy. I think it should!" Meanwhile, "The Original Series" and "The Animated Series" writer David Gerrold said he felt that debates about canon are silly:

"All this argument about canon is stupid. It has Gene Roddenberry's name on it. It has William Shatner as Kirk, it has Leonard Nimoy as Spock, it has [DeForest] Kelley as McCoy, it has Jimmy Doohan as Scotty, it has Majel Barrett as Nurse Chapel, it has Nichelle Nichols as Uhura, it has George Takei as Sulu."

Likewise, when "The Animated Series" initially aired, it didn't really undermine what had been laid down by "The Original Series." Rather, it was the "Star Trek" shows and movies that came after it that led to problems. That sounds like canon to me.

Indeed, many details from "Star Trek: The Animated Series" have since found their way into the live-action canon, like how James Kirk's middle name is Tiberius (as he clarifies in the "Animated Series" episode "Bem"). And though presented as a novel invention on "Star Trek: The Next Generation," the holodeck first appeared in the "Animated Series" episode "The Practical Joker."

In keeping with this, the show "Star Trek: Enterprise" incorporates several elements of "The Animated Series" into the mix. Specifically, a Sehlat — a Vulcan creature that serves as Spock's childhood pet in the "Animated Series" episode "Yesteryear" — appears in the "Enterprise" episode "The Forge." The "Enterprise" episode "The Catwalk" similarly confirms that Vulcans go on a desert-bound maturation ritual when they are children known as the kahs-wan, a term that was first spoken in, you guessed it, "Yesteryear."

And that's to mention nothing of the animated show "Star Trek: Lower Decks," which integrates myriad details and Easter eggs alluding to "The Animated Series." The latter show may be somewhat forgotten these days, but it's certainly worth revisiting (or watching for the very first time) and remains central to so much of the rest of the "Star Trek" mythology.

#3459. How to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6

There's the easy way and the expensive way

There's the easy way and the expensive way

It doesn't take long for one of your cars to end up at the police impound in Grand Theft Auto 6. You might have abandoned it near a crime scene, or they arrested you while you were driving it. While the circumstances may vary, you have only two ways to proceed if a car is impounded: you forget about it or you retrieve it.

If you are not ready to abandon your favorite car and want it back, we've got you covered. Here's how to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6.

There are two methods to retrieve a car from the police impound: you can either steal it back or pay for it. Both are valid, but the second one becomes available only in Chapter 2.

Stealing the car is the most plausible and cheapest option to execute. You just need to head to the impound lot, enter, and drive your car away from there. Some impounds, like the one in Port Gellhorn, have openings that you can use to enter unnoticed. Regardless of how you get inside, the challenge is escaping from the police once you leave. You must be prepared to run away, so try to come up with an escape route by setting a destination far from the city.

Now, the second option requires the Scooter Bros app, which you unlock in Chapter 2 after completing Moses' mission. If you have it already, open the app and select the impounded car (the one with a police badge icon). You will see that the first option in the menu is to pay a fee to retrieve the car.

The price varies depending on how far you are from the police impound. For example, I would have to pay $699 to get my car back from the Port Gellhorn impound while in Vice City. However, if you have upgraded your Scooter Bros account to Premium, you can use your remaining daily credits to request an impounded vehicle. Since this will essentially consume all your credits for the day, you should wait until you have only one left before using this option.

Sometimes, two franchises can blend together rather synergetically to create a thrilling new tale worth following. In the case of DC Comics, the latest iteration of this has been Green Lantern: Doomed Cosmos, blending the mythology and iconic characters of DC with the grim darkness and far future aesthetics of Warhammer 40,000. Even though this isn't an official partnership, it still blends each aesthetic rather beautifully thanks in large part to illustrator Kyle Hotz. The series already underwent its reveal a month ago, but recent solicits and glimpses for Green Lantern: Doomed Cosmos #2 hint at not just the Green Lantern Corps' new look at new angles, but the similarly-styled legions launched against them.

With issue #1 teasing the Empire of Humanity's reign of terror across the cosmos bringing the lone human Hal Jordan to join the Green Lantern Corps, Green Lantern: Doomed Cosmos #2 adds even more terror on multiple fronts. Original glimpses had fans seeing legions of what resembled the Order of St. and countless Azraels bearing down on the Corps, but now Humanity has unleashed a deadly new legion based on Batman, while the Thanagarians kick the hopeless situation up a notch, branded as traitors by the Green Lanterns. With Hal joined by fellow Green Lanterns Thaal Sinestro, Kilowog, Salaak, and Tomar-Re, it appears they'll have to fight, rip, and tear their way through in order for the cosmos to have hope for peace.

As if the gorgeous variant artwork such as by Björn Barends wasn't enough from the last issue, new glimpses of Green Lantern: Doomed Cosmos give new looks at the various armor options for Hal as well as the aesthetics of his opponents. Lieutenants Jordan, Sinestro, and Kilowog regroup on a Green Lantern Corps friend-ly planet with the rest of their unit only to find themselves backed into a hellish, gore-filled corner. The wretched armadas of humanity rain fiery death down from above in the form of humanity's black ops unit, the Dark Knights — unyielding and brutal killers who utilize the most profane tactics to strike fear into alien hearts. Someone up there must really hate Hal Jordan!!

Hal Jordan, exploding corpse bombs, hellish Batmen, aliens, living spaceships, and magnificent green gun-fueled violence await!

Meanwhile, the Chris Mooneyham variant showcases a heavier wash of green hues, as what appears to be a helmeted Hal warns of the Thanagarian traitors swooping in from above. In terms of creating a story largely involving warfare waged across the stars, the war-like Thanagarians are a natural addition, while the Batmen of the Dark Knights are an absolute crowd-pleaser, begging the question of what armies there are to follow.

Given the Dark Knights and Thanagarians are featuring in Green Lantern: Doomed Cosmos as antagonistic factions against the outgunned Green Lantern Corps, it seems fair to suspect other friendly faces might appear opposite Hal soon. The Empire of Humanity would likely feature other Justice League mainstays and their aesthetics emulated across entire armies of their own, which is already an enticing idea. But with the series set to launch on January 20, 2027, with issue #2 on the way for February 17, 2027, fans will just wait to see what Green Lantern: Doomed Cosmos has in store.

Blade Runner 2049, in my humble opinion, is a science-fiction masterpiece. The Denis Villeneuve-directed sequel not only expertly builds upon Ridley Scott’s 1982 film, but it also adds to the mythology in interesting ways. Additionally, the film includes a stellar performance from Harrison Ford, who reprises his role as Rick Deckard. In the near decade since the film’s release, I’ve been wondering about Deckard’s ultimate fate. So, when CinemaBlend spoke to the creator of Blade Runner 2099, I asked for her take.

Deckard serves as more of a supporting character in Villeneuve’s heavily praised film, which reveals the former Blade Runner to be in hiding in the ruins of Las Vegas 30 years after the events of the OG film. Found by Replicant Runner K (Ryan Gosling), Deckard is eventually revealed to have fathered a child with his late replicant partner, Rachel. That child is eventually revealed to be replicant-memory-maker Dr. Ana Stelline (Carla Juri), with whom Deckard reunites at the end of the film, thanks to K.

Since walking out of the theater after seeing the film for the first time in 2017, I’ve wondered about Deckard and Ana’s fates, especially with the looming war between humans and Replicants. Blade Runner 2099 creator/showrunner Silka Luisa is also a major fan of the franchise and, when she was asked for her take on what happened to Ana and Deckard, she shared some surprising comments with CB:

I never asked Michael Green, because I'm sure — he was the screenwriter for 2049, and there's just no world [where] he didn't know what happens. But I almost didn't want to know. What I love about Blade Runner is that so much of it can exist in your own mind, and the world feels so rich that it inspires you to create your own stories within it. And something about that period not being totally defined is exciting, because we can all suggest different things. Yeah, so I don't have a definitive answer.

Considering how big a Blade Runner fan Luisa is, I’m honestly shocked over her not asking Michael Green (who shares 2049 writing credits with Hampton Fancher) for a definitive answer on Deckard and Ana. I can, however, also see Luisa’s point, though, as this franchise does leave certain plot threads open-ended, leading to fan speculation. This answer also tracks with the EP’s approach to 2099, which is a standalone piece that doesn’t have direct references to its big-screen predecessors.

While Blade Runner’s ending remains controversial in some circles, the discussions surrounding 2049’s conclusion arguably aren’t as tense. Villeneuve’s film went through different alterations during development, and even the ending changed. Fancher previously disclosed that the original plan was for Deckard to die. While that could’ve been powerful (if crafted effectively), I’m fine with Deckard not biting the big one, considering it leaves the door open for a direct sequel. And Silka Luisa is down for that as well:

I really hope they make another. I really hope they make a sequel, just as a fan, to be honest.

For right now, though, fans can return to this dark, futuristic universe by way of 2099. The limited series centers on dying Replicant Blade Runner Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human posing as a Replicant. While fans won’t be getting answers on Deckard, the show covers plenty of ground in other respects. And, who knows, maybe we’ll actually get that 2049 sequel one day.

All episodes of Blade Runner 2099 will begin streaming for Prime Video subscription holders on November 25 amid the 2026 TV schedule. Blade Runner 2049 can also currently be streamed on Prime, and it’s available to watch for free on Tubi.

#3456. How To Watch You Can See Everything At Home

Just when you thought the Elizabeth Holmes saga had run its course, a wild Nathan Fielder once again appears. There's a good reason why critics (including /Film's own Ethan Anderton) called "You Can See Everything" a mind-melting masterwork and arguably the movie of the year. The documentary blurs the lines between fact and fiction, interviewer and subject, and pretty much every other binary you can think of — and, yes, that's only barely exaggerating. Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim truly pulled off something special here, to the extent that the film broke containment and managed to get even rubbernecking general audiences interested enough to result in expectation-defying success at the box office.

Now, viewers at home will get the chance to experience (or re-experience) this chaotic journey for themselves. After indie studio A24 sat back and enjoyed its bank-breaking run in theaters, "You Can See Everything" is finally available to lie, scheme, charm, and manipulate its way into your own living room. (Note: If any distinctively blonde, blue-eyed, deep-voiced, AI-generated images of a certain infamous businesswoman end up coming along for the ride, uh, we suggest running the other way.) Indeed, you can currently watch the film digitally, and the PVOD format allows you to rent or purchase copies from all the usual online retailers, ranging from Apple to Amazon to Fandango at Home.

For those eager to fall down this Theranos-sized rabbit hole even more, well, there's good news on that front, too.

Can't get enough of the documentary sensation that's all but guaranteed to have a clear path to the Oscars? Us, neither. Fans will soon be able to keep the good times going at home as "You Can See Everything" enters the next stage of its lifecycle. Think of it this way: for weeks, we've had to make do with fuzzy screenshots, gifs and clips from trailers, and other measures of last resort to discuss this meme-factory of a movie. Now, we can do all that all over again, but this time with the crystal-clear clarity that comes with 4K digital releases.

But that's not all. As an A24 release, and as part of the company's deal with the former Warner Bros. Discovery, we can expect "You Can See Everything" to come to streaming on HBO Max at a to-be-announced date in the near future, followed by what's sure to be a buzzy home media release on 4K UHD, Blu-ray, and DVD. The surrealistic docudrama has already outperformed al reasonable expectations by this point (especially if/when it sets its sights on Academy gold), but this will have every chance to experience a very long tail as more and more viewers discover this movie without ever needing to leave their living rooms.

Between this, Hulu's "The Dropout," and the nonfiction book "Bad Blood" documenting how the real-life story went down, it's safe to say Holmes enthusiasts (if you want to call yourselves that) will be busy for quite some time.

As Inside the NBA’s latest season on ESPN continues, questions continue to swirl around the show in regard to its future. Longtime co-host Ernie Johnson has officially confirmed his plans to leave the show at the end of this season, and colleague Charles Barkley apparently plans to do the same. There’s been a lot of discussion regarding who might replace the beloved sports commentators, and Barkley recently pitched his successor. While it’s a solid pick, I’d admittedly prefer to see another seasoned pundit take over Barkley’s post.

Barkley – also known as “The Round Mound of Rebound” to some – is definitely someone who loves to speak his mind. So it doesn’t surprise me at all that he’d have thoughts on who might be able to take his place on Inside. The former Phoenix Sun was recently quoted as saying he didn’t believe anyone but fellow ex-player Jalen Rose could replace him at the desk. That comment was brought up to Rose when he was interviewed by Front Office Sports (as seen on YouTube) and, when asked about the job, he said this:

I love Charles and yes, that would be something that I would be interested in. The one thing I learned about this business is everything isn't transactional. If Charles Barkley is going to say into a microphone that you're the person that he feels like should replace him, you can't write a check for that. Even if it never happens. And so, for him to say that, it's priceless. I'm so very gracious.

The notion of Rose taking over for Barkley is actually quite reasonable, considering his resume as a broadcaster. He’s not only served as a fill-in analyst for Inside the NBA for years now, but he’s also taken on hosting duties for ABC/ESPN over the years. I personally enjoy seeing Rose when he appears on Inside, and his relaxed demeanor usually serves as a firm counterbalance to others on the dais like the vivacious Barkley or Shaquille O’Neal. With that said, there’s another recurring analyst I’d love to see join the show instead.

Inside has welcomed plenty of insightful and entertaining guest hosts over the years, from the cool Vince Carter to the wise-cracking Draymond Green (who has a rivalry with Charles Barkley). Someone who, for me, has always been a welcome presence on the show is Chris Webber, who’s been appearing on the show for years. He obviously has plenty of broadcasting experience, and he’s a wealth of knowledge when it comes to basketball. I’d say the show would be lucky to have him full-time.

Again, though, this isn’t to say that Jalen Rose wouldn’t be able to do the job effectively. There may actually be a reality in which both players end up on the show full time by next season. However, that’s assuming ESPN is looking to bring on two former players and not get another non-ex-player analyst to specifically fill the void that’ll be left by Johnson.

To be honest, it may also behoove me not to get too ahead of myself right now, as the season is still young. Also, while Charles Barkley’s retirement claim is seeming more likely, he hasn’t said much more about it in the wake of Ernie Johnson’s announcement. We’ll just have to wait and see what happens and how the producers choose to proceed should Barkley leave the fold along with Johnson.

Check out Inside the NBA when it returns to NBA on Wednesday, November 25 amid the 2026 TV schedule.

#3454. Rings Of Power Season 3 Shows Why Canon Is Not Important In Lord Of The Rings

Keep it secret, keep it safe ... from spoilers. This article discusses major plot details from "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" up through to Season 3, Episode 6.

As an adaptation, "The Rings of Power" is possibly the most polarizing thing to come out of J.R.R. Tolkien's Legendarium in decades. From characters created specifically for the series to its portrayal of fan-favorites like Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), and its tweaks to Tolkien's Middle-earth lore, the show is full of creative elements that have proven controversial. That hasn't changed over time, either, as "The Rings of Power" Season 3 is now adding a love triangle, a new origin story for the Nazgûl, and a meeting between Sauron (Charlie Vickers) and a Balrog (Simon Pegg) to the pile (via IGN). Suffice it to say, these alternations have angered some fans who feel the series is deviating from the canon and, as such, Tolkien's intent.

Now, canon is one of the biggest battlefronts of the internet fandom wars, which (as ridiculous as they are) themselves have only grown as big franchises continue to dominate the entertainment landscape. As a result, lots of online conversations now center on how, say, a "Star Wars" TV series deviates from books written in the 1990s or how a movie like this year's "Resident Evil" fits into the larger property's timeline. But whenit comes to "The Rings of Power," it's even sillier since the show has to please fans of both Tolkien's books and Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" movies alike (even though Jackson's films themselves make substantial modifications to their source material).

Here's the thing, though: Ultimately, canon is not important, especially when it comes to "Lord of the Rings."

Middle-earth has a vast and detailed history spanning thousands of years. And yet, J.R.R. Tolkien technically only published two stories in his lifetime: "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings." So, when it comes to the proper "canon" of Middle-earth, that's really all there is to it. Sure, Tolkien's appendices introduce concepts such as the tale of Númenor, for example. But all the First Age stuff like the War of Wrath and the Silmarils, Morgoth and Sauron's history, and the larger saga of Arda all came from, essentially, scribbles and notes by Tolkien that were only published posthumously.

Moreover, another thing that makes Middle-earth's mythology so unique is that Tolkien's notes are full of inconsistencies and retcons. Indeed, there are many issues that Tolkien was able to fully make up his mind about, like the origin of the orcs and whether they are inherently and absolutely evil or not. Likewise, Tolkien struggled with whether to keep his original idea of Middle-earth having been a flat world that eventually turned into a spherical planet (after the fall of Númenor), and he never settled on an answer.

It wasn't just that, either. Much like George Lucas has changed the original "Star Wars" trilogy with every new re-release, Tolkien went back and forth on his writing about Middle-earth throughout his lifetime. In the end, he made tons of revisions big and small to the reprints of his "Lord of the Rings" books.

If J.R.R. Tolkien himself never got around to delivering a complete and finished version of his "canon," then why should fans fight about it? If we should take one thing away from the professor's work, it's that he thought his own fictional universe was malleable, and nothing was set in stone until the last minute. He and George Lucas are far from the only creatives to take this approach, either. For that matter, something as worlds apart as "The Simpsons" is constantly tweaking its own "canon" (with one exception).

This is not to say that we should simply discard everything that has come before and hit the reset button with every new entry in a franchise. Consistency is important, but it's equally vital not to let new ideas be limited by what came before. "The Rings of Power" may be adding things that Tolkien never wrote, but it's giving us Sauron clashing with a Balrog, and isn't that idea just too cool to pass up? More than any other property, "Lord of the Rings" doesn't have an expanded universe that's set in stone, anyway. Rather, it's always morphed to incorporate fresh ideas to some degree, so why stop now?

"The Rings of Power" has many issues, especially when it comes to its pacing. That said, it's always done a good job of reinterpreting its source material in a way that captures the essence of Tolkien's ideals while integrating exciting concepts we haven't seen in this franchise before. Stream in on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

I'm not sure I would've ever expected William Shatner to be mentioned in the same breath as Grand Theft Auto VI, but that's what's been happening as of late. A viral clip recently showed Shatner besmirching the recently released game, and it generated a bit of backlash. Now, Shatner is speaking out about the brouhaha. Frankly, I'm surprised the 95-year-old actor even knew what it was, and based on his latest comments, I'm still unsure whether he does.

As Star Trek fans may be well aware, Shatner is relatively unafraid to offer an opinion on subjects he's not completely familiar with. He's landed in hot water before offering up tons of commentary on Trek, despite never watching the shows, and now, a clip of him talking about the game on Piers Morgan Uncensored is making waves. The host prompted Shatner for his opinion on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he said the following:

No! I think it's the dumbest thing I've ever heard! Why don't you read a good book?

As one might expect, some people took offense to Shatner and other commentators' words on the program. This is, after all, a game that has made more than Taylor Swift's Eras tour in under a week. Comments on the clip popped up on X, and they were critical of all involved:

The comments called out various claims, mainly the assertion that Grand Theft Auto VI is simply a "pimp simulator." Of course, it was previously announced that the game would not allow prostitution, which was featured in previous releases.

William Shatner seemed to catch wind of the negative comments and was quick to respond on his personal X account. He wanted to say that his comments were not meant to be inflammatory to the game or gamers, but rather to the four panelists that he had to sit and watch before doing his own segment:

Last week there were a bucketful of nasty replies on this video clip where most of the angry “children” took the quote as a general statement but didn’t bother to see what I was referring to as ridiculous. Prior to my segment, there was a segment on GTA. Look at these 4 that got airtime 👇🏻! 🙄 Unfortunately, they probably don’t know how to read, especially the guy in 🕶️. That’s who they got to represent gamers. That’s what the comment was about. I had to suffer watching them it was ridiculous! 😤😑

I'm hoping Shatner isn't stressed about this, because I know I'm not personally concerned about what opinion he holds on Grand Theft Auto VI. In fact, I would expect most people north of 90 years old would not be too interested in video games and would sooner read a book.

What I am interested in, however, are William Shatner's thoughts on past co-stars and what he has to say about space and life in general. Fortunately, he's often doing that as well as making frequent trips around the world to talk to anyone who will listen about his past feuds and time in Hollywood.

Grand Theft Auto VI is available to purchase right now, and William Shatner is frequently on the web offering up his opinion. I'm honestly still tickled that this whole situation even happened, and I love it when two pieces of pop culture I love intersect in an unexpected way.

Mick Joest is a Content Producer for CinemaBlend with his hand in an eclectic mix of television goodness. He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3451. Vice City portal Easter egg location in GTA 6

How to open the portal to the original Vice City

How to open the portal to the original Vice City

The Vice City portal Easter egg is a unique event in Grand Theft Auto 6 that lets you travel through time. It might not look like it, but the existence of a secret portal in Leonida is quite plausible, considering the UFOs appearing in the skies and the forgotten haunted hotels you can visit.

To experience this event and open the portal, you will have to complete a long series of steps. But don't worry, below, we explain everything you need to know to complete the Vice City portal Easter egg in GTA 6.

If you want to start the Vice City portal event in GTA 6, you must travel to Key Lento, the initial area in the game, and head to the Badger radio tower, northeast of the Nifty Threads Island Wear shop. Enter the tower and climb to the top to reach what appears to be a control room.

Beside the door, there's a lever. Pull it up then press the button on the panel near the old television. If you've done everything correctly, the TV will turn on and display the word "Malibu." Now, leave the tower and prepare for the next step.

After you have finished the initial ratio tower step, you will need to visit 12 LPL substations around Leonidas following a specific order. There will be a letter or two on the outer wall of each substation, which will form a secret message when all 12 letters are put together. In each one, you will find either a button or a lever that represents a letter or symbol. To ensure you're interacting with the correct one, check the pink tape near the button/lever and look for the letter/symbol it features.

Before you start, keep in mind that you can't fast travel using the RydeMe app or swap between characters. Doing so resets the mission, and you will need to return to the radio tower to start it again. You'll know that you have completed this step when you receive a message from an unknown contact after you pull up the last lever. Below, we listed the substations in the order you must visit them, where you will find the button or lever you must activate, and which letter they represent.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — Southwest corner of Downtown, just southwest of Zenith gym.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — West side of Balsero, just northwest of Randy's shop.

Location: Key Lento (Mariana County) —Northwest of Kenton's shop

Location: Vice Beach (Vice-Dale County) — North side of Penmarch Isle.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — West side of Bayside, just northwest of the Vice City apartment.

Location: Port Gellhorn (Kelly County) — North of Moses' shop.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) — East of Big Shot Ammu-Nation shop​​​​​​​.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — Northwest area of Gloriana Key.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) - East side of Hamlet, just northeast of the Boone Speedway.

Location: Gellhorn (Kelly County) — Northeast of Raceway.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) - South side of Hamlet, just southeast of Boone Speedway and the Pay 'N' Spray.

Location: North Mariana County (Mariana County) — South of Breakwater Quarry

If you combine all the letters, you'll get the message: Life is passing me by, which is a PC cheat code that allows you to speed up time in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

The final step in the event requires you to follow the instructions in the message you receive after activating the 12th lever: head to the T. H. Power Station, east of Hamlet in Vice-Dale County, between 7 p.m. and 6 a.m. Once there, you will find the portal that will take you to the original Vice City.

You can find the portal on the north side of the power station. You'll know you're at the right place if you can see traces of energy from the portal running through the cables in the area. Reaching the portal might be difficult, considering how heavily guarded the area is. Consider either using a helicopter or swimming around the area to find a good entry point.

Once you find the portal, pull the lever on the left side of the gate, and you'll be teleported. To leave the original Vice City, just head to the room behind the bar, and you will be back to the world of GTA 6. By completing this event, you will receive Tony Vercetti's Hawaiian shirt, the American Glory motorcycle (don't forget to register it!), and unlock a new livery for purchase at Vice Vinyl.

If you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. Check out our GTA 6 beginner guide to get a grasp of the basics and our tips for what to do first, recommendations for the best ways to make money fast, and an explainer for how to keep stolen weapons and cars to make the most of your free time.

Our selection of GTA 6 guides includes help for things like how to steal the Phoenix in "Unwanted Attention" and whether you should defuse Mandy, too. There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

Remember, folks: People will come and go, life will always find a way to kick you while you're down, but the whale? The whale is forever. Ever since the project was first announced, "Whalefall" remained a fixture in our most anticipated film of 2026 ... and the movie adaptation most definitely lived up to the hype, at least according to, uh, myself. Who wouldn't be interested in the story of a scuba diver with some serious daddy issues getting caught up in a life-or-death struggle between a sperm whale and a squid, ending up swallowed whole by the aforementioned whale, and needing to find a way to escape before his oxygen supply runs out? Though the original Daniel Kraus novel was previously considered an unadaptable work, writer/director Brian Duffield found a way, and the results speak for themselves.

Of course, that was the experience of watching "Whalefall" on the big screen. What about at home? Fans who found themselves gasping for breath, shielding their eyes, and otherwise staving off panic attacks in theaters (or was that just me?) can now see if the experience translates to the comforting confines of your own living room. 20th Century Studios has announced that "Whalefall" will swim towards a digital PVOD release on December 1, 2026. Those who rent or purchase a digital copy from the online retailer of their choice will also get an exclusive bonus feature (a terrible home media trend we've spoken out on before) in the form of a "Creature Design Audio Commentary" featuring production designer Ramsey Avery and VFX supervisor Guillaume Rocheron.

Fortunately, viewers can look forward to the film's upcoming release on physical media early in the new year as well.

The ambitious film that once again puts poor Austin Abrams through the wringer after this year's "Resident Evil" won't just be available to watch at home in less time than it takes to be digested by a whale (don't quote me on that fact), it will also come loaded with extras, bonus features, and other goodies for the eager film enthusiast. #3449. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finale Explained: The Doom Of Men Begins

Warning! Spoilers for Rings of Power season 3, episode 8, ahead!The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 ends with a major victory for the race of Men. For most of this installment in the Prime Video fantasy series, it has been the Elves who have been stuck in terrible, bloody conflict with the Dark Lord. The War of the Elves and Sauron had been raging for five years by the start of season 3, and there was minimal help from the other races of Middle-earth. That all finally changes in Rings of Power season 3's penultimate episode when Pharazôn finally decides to answer the Elves' call.

Unfortunately for the Elves and Men gearing up to hit the battlefield, Pharazôn decided to intervene just as Sauron finished forging his One Ring to Rule Them All. This meant the Elves had no choice but to remove their Three, and the influence of the Nine and Seven is that much stronger. Sauron also successfully built forces in all the right places of Middle-earth to ensure that the Elves and Númenóreans were outnumbered and hopelessly cornered. Overall, things just weren't looking so hopeful.

Thanks to Gandalf and the Dark Wizard (AKA Pallando), a bit of good was spread through the atmosphere and the cultists from Rhün—the Dark Wizards' followers—turned their backs and headed home. This, paired with a personal challenge from Pharazôn, left Sauron feeling a bit less certain of victory than he seemingly had before. Still, the tables weren't quite turned enough for Sauron to do what he did next in the finale of The Rings of Power season 3. For some remarkable reason, Sauron surrendered to Pharazôn, and the battle ended before it even started.

It's clear by the end of The Rings of Power season 3 that Pharazôn believes he has just won a great victory without even trying. In the king's eyes, he is so frightening and marvelous that even the Dark Lord Sauron just presented himself to him on his knees. Of course, that evil smile on Sauron's face in the finale's last seconds definitively proves there is a lot more going on here. Indeed, the Dark Lord would never give up so easily after having just finally completed his master weapon. There's a deeper plan.

Sauron is a deceiver and manipulator, and it doesn't take much to see in Rings of Power that Pharazôn is precisely the sort of man who will easily buy into flattery. The looks on Gil-galad's, Elrond's, Galadriel's, and Celeborn's faces make it clear that they know for absolutely certain that something is wrong. They would never trust taking Sauron into custody when he goes so willingly. They also know that nothing they say will keep Pharazôn from fully embracing this apparent victory. Sauron just ceded the title of King of Men, and Pharazôn will take it.

This really leaves only one reason Sauron would hand himself over to Pharazôn—he wants to get closer to him. The War of the Elves of Sauron had gone past the point of deception. There was nothing to do but dominate on the battlefield. Now that Númenor has joined the fight and Sauron has lost a chunk of his forces, the villain must lean back on his greatest skill. It's time to turn on the charm, and this will bring nothing but doom to Pharazôn and his men as Rings of Power continues.

When Sauron was joined in Mordor by the forces of Rhûn, they brought Gandalf and the Dark Wizard with them. Previously in Rings of Power season 3, the Grey Wizard learned from the Secret Fire itself that his job wasn't to defeat the Dark Wizard, but to save him. The big opportunity finally arrives in the finale as Sauron gives Pallando one of his Nine Rings, offering to make him a Witch-king that no Man can slay. Pallando accepts this offer, but a little Tomfoolery on Gandalf's part allows him to pretty easily remove the Ring from his old friend's hand.

Freed of the Dark Lord's influence and inspired by Gandalf's determination that their role is only ever to spread goodness and hope through Middle-earth, Pallando rejoins the good guys. These two wizards face off against one of Saruon's Nazgnagôl, and though they are ultimately successful in throwing him from Barad-dûr, Pallando takes a fatal stab to the torso. Gandalf holds his friend as his soul passes back to Valinor.

That's when things really get interesting. Pallando's soul or essence seems to shoot out from his body in an aurora of light that spreads across Mordor. When the swirls of color land on the Dark Wizard's followers, they drop their weapons, turn, and walk away. It seems that Pallando was able to do some good in the end after all. With this more positive influence, Sauron lost a massive chunk of his army in a single turn.

After saying his goodbyes to Pallando in The Rings of Power season 3's finale, Gandalf decides to head back West to meet with the Elves. As he goes, he is reunited with none other than Tom Bombadil, who accompanies him. What's especially strange about this (even more so than Tom Bombadil typically makes things) is that when Gandalf presented Old Tom with the burden of Pallando's Ring, Tom made the evil thing disappear entirely.

In Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, Sauron's One Ring had no influence on Tom Bombadil. Still, there was no indication that he could have ever just made it disappear without any further fuss. This isn't even the most troublesome part, however, since the mystery here is how Sauron will successfully appoint all Nine of his Nazgûl if he now has only eight rings. Whatever Tom did to handle that Ring, it's certainly not a solution that will last forever.

Now that Sauron has handed himself over to the men of Númenor in The Rings of Power season 3, the tides of the war have changed. In a way, the Elves just won the War of the Elves and Sauron, though it's a pretty bitter victory. It will be clear to them that Sauron has something up his sleeve, but there is almost no chance that Pharazôn will hear them out—not while he can claim to be so frightening that even the Dark Lord fell to his knees before him. Now, more likely than not, Sauron will be brought back to Númenor, and that won't bode well for anyone.

Sauron's captivity in Númenor in The Rings of Power season 3 opens the door wide to the next stage in Tolkien's canon. Throughout this entire prequel series, the Dark Lord, whether as Halbrand, Annatar, or Sauron, has been rather fascinated with Númenor. He wants some of these Men to wear his Rings, but, more than that, he wants to see them conquered and controlled across the board. Pharazôn's hubris will be punished, and the great wave that Rings of Power has been foreshadowing since day one is just around the corner.

In a surprising reveal, Arnold Schwarzenegger’s son, Joseph Baena, has announced that he’ll be in the upcoming Baywatch reboot. Primarily known for his previous appearance as a contestant in Season 31 of Dancing with the Stars, his background in bodybuilding and his physique make it a no-brainer that he’s found his way onto the beach.

Since hearing about the upcoming Baywatch reboot, Baena wanted to get in on the action. And while he didn’t get the opportunity to audition until the show had already started and the slow motion-running was already in full swing, he was able to snag an appearance in one of the 12 episodes that will debut in January 2027. While on set to shoot an episode of Celebrity Weakest Link, he told Us Magazine:

I’m Livvy Dunne’s boyfriend in the show. And she was amazing — such a great talent and she was such a talented and special gymnast. To see her in Baywatch was great.

Upon joining Baywatch’s cast, model Livvy Dunne put on one of the iconic red swimsuits and got to work alongside the OGs, also making appearances. It sounds like Joseph Baena was quite impressed with the work the cast has put in.

If the BTS Baywatch content is any indication, the cast of the reboot, who were already physically fit, has been going through rigorous training to not only prepare for their roles, but to maintain that strength and endurance for an entire season. Baena’s own dedication to fitness and training had him working out with them on set too. He said:

She killed it. As did the rest of the cast. Thaddeus [LaGrone], Noah Beck and everyone else is doing a phenomenal job. It was amazing to spend time with them on set and work out with them on set. I’m just really excited for the episode to come out of the whole show.

The 29-year-old half-sibling of Patrick Schwarzenegger admitted he didn’t watch the original Baywatch series when it premiered on TV. Instead, he became a fan of David Hasselhoff when he was in the SpongeBob movie, where there was a playful homage to the show and his character.

While we don’t know much about Joseph Baena’s role in the Baywatch reboot, we do know that he’s playing a character named Pete, the boyfriend of Grace. Without any details about the kind of relationship they have, he made his hope for a Season 2 return very clear. He explained:

We have to make the plot line [happen]. I get that — in the first season — they need to establish everyone. Maybe in the second season they can have a little fun and bring Pete back.

Since we’ve only seen glimpses and teases of footage, it’s hard to get a sense of the show’s tone, the new character dynamics, and just how epic the action will be on a weekly basis. However, with the new generation of lifeguards being led by Hobie (Stephen Amell), the son of the iconic Mitch Buchannon (David Hasselhoff), and a number of the OG cast members returning, the hype and the nostalgia are real and should easily get an audience tuning in.

Obviously, a second season and beyond is never a guarantee, but if Baywatch does get to continue, I actually think it would be pretty fun to see characters, even those with small appearances, return in the future. When you see someone rescued pop up again, or you get to see more of a relationship play out, like with Dunne's Grace and Baena’s Pete, it helps ground a TV series, especially with one as big as Baywatch is sure to be.

No matter how it all plays out, I know I’ll be tuning in to see how it all goes down with Hobie and all the new lifeguards of this highly anticipated reboot. And yes, I'm also looking forward to seeing Baena on the beach too.

#3447. Hexed Review: A Safe And Solidly Witchy Disney Original

Some of us grew up dreaming of becoming princesses and knights in fairy tales, others of becoming astronauts (or in my case, uh, the guy who gets to drive the garbage truck). Only the coolest — and weirdest — kids among us imagined themselves slapping on some eyeshadow, living it up from atop flying brooms, and casting gnarly spells. Who else but witches can transform the rigidly bland world around us into one positively teeming with magic and color and life?

The wish-fulfillment of it all probably explains why this makes for such a neat premise in a movie like "Hexed" ... even if that potential isn't fully realized. Disney's latest animated original, from directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand and co-director Josie Trinidad, is mostly content to play things safe and deliver a fairly predictable coming-of-age story. While this family-friendly, PG-rated romp doesn't linger too much on the darkness inherent in witches, there's an undeniable undercurrent of something much more provocative at work.

Because being a witch isn't all fun and games. Along with strong personalities and powers beyond compare, they also come with the baggage of being profoundly misunderstood. Their curse is to be loners, outcasts, and pariahs, forever looking for a coven to call their own. Whenever the script by co-writers Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller fully leans into this, embodied by misfit high schooler Billie Doe (voiced by the always-capable Hailee Steinfeld) in search of a deeper sense of belonging, "Hexed" takes on a life of its own. When relying on frenetic pacing and joke-a-minute thrills to sweep us along and glide past any discomfort, it struggles to come together.

There's a greater movie somewhere inside "Hexed," just waiting to break free. Instead, we're left with a safe and solid enough adventure that could've been something more.

Right from the opening exposition dump of "Hexed," we're taken through a prototypical backstory of how witches were chased out of "normal" society and forced to create a mystical refuge of their own called Hexe. Unfortunately, the founding witch died before she could complete this new utopia, dooming her followers to wait for the prophesied "Chosen One" to cast a spell known only to themselves and restore everyone's powers to their fullest. ("The foretelling was foretold," as numerous characters amusingly reference this event.)

This intersects neatly with Billie's arc, our rule-breaking teenager with latent witchy powers whose mother Alice (the rather obvious voice-casting of Rashida Jones) has hidden away from the world and from her supposed destiny. When Billie's abilities manifest as an infant and nearly spirit her away to Hexe, Alice takes great pains to hide her daughter's true origins from herself — even to the point of moving out of Salem altogether and into the blandest, most unassuming place on Earth to pass as an unremarkable normie (Ohio). All in all, it's a pretty standard setup for a parable about identity, puberty, and being yourself (alongside a hint of queer subtext), which "Hexed" pulls off with the appropriate amount of emotional, tear-jerker aplomb.

But otherwise, this is largely an excuse to show off the film's stunning world-building prowess. Yes, Hexe oftentimes tends to resemble Universal's Wizarding World of Harry Potter. But once Billie finally makes it to this living and breathing realm — marked by an expanding aspect ratio to soak in the full scope of Hexe — and assembles unlikely allies like an enchanted pot, Walton Goggins' cat-like and delightfully-named familiar Beef Roger Crummchuk, and neurotic owl Nigel (Henry Winkler), you'll never want to leave this kaleidoscopic wonderland.

Where "Hexed" struggles most, ironically, is in its attempt to carve out a niche for itself amid the vast canon of Disney's animated movies. On one hand, it's strangely fitting for a story about individualism to be so preoccupied by what's come before. On the other, it has the side effect of triggering a tangible identity crisis. At this point, Disney's house-style CG animation has been set in stone and nothing here diverges all that much from the likes of "Frozen" — down to the look of the film's main villain Queen Celeste, brought to life by a scenery-chewing Jodie Foster. Elsewhere, some of the imagery of Hexe itself feel cribbed from classics like "Cinderella" or "Fantasia," coming across less like a loving homage and more like a copy of a copy. Even Kris Bowers' distinctive score is overshadowed by a parade of on-the-nose needle drops, from Queen to Dua Lipa.

This has the cumulative effect of making "Hexed" an oddly meta experience, in a way that both livens things up and makes for a somewhat awkward addition to the Disney pantheon. Much of the humor comes from the script's winking self-awareness and its many "Can you believe this?" visual gags, which could've fell flat on their face but instead (mostly) work. But even its most inspired moments of creativity and imagination feel undercut by a script that's either unwilling or unable to push such boundaries beyond its most surface-level joys.

Still, parents could do far worse than "Hexed" when it comes to movies their children will inevitably re-watch a million times over once it comes to Disney+. While that might seem like damning with faint praise, it does speak to the basics of storytelling that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn, Jason Hand, and Josie Trinidad manage to get right — especially within a noticeably tight, 103-minute runtime. For all intents and purposes, this breezy storyline might as well be designed to function like a runaway train, constantly keeping the action at a sprinter's pace and hardly giving young viewers a chance to catch their breath. Even the "camera" stays in motion at almost all times and makes the few, much-needed moments of respite and quiet conversation stand out all the more.

This "Get in, get out" approach at least provides a jolt of energy right from the get-go and carries the emotions along with it, even if it can occasionally get exhausting. At its heart, "Hexed" lives or dies by the mother/daughter bond forged between impulsive Billie and overbearing Alice, and its best moments soar as direct result of never losing sight of these two characters.

There are plenty of narrative holes left oddly unexplained and an unfortunate bit of sequel-bait sweatiness to contend with, likely included in the off-chance this kills it at the box office. (This raises another question, of course: Was holding this Halloween-friendly movie about spooky witches closer to the extended Thanksgiving holiday weekend really worth it?) But thanks to dazzling visuals, a strong emotional undercurrent, and killer world-building, "Hexed" is a solid — if safe — family outing.

"Hexed" opens in theaters on November 25, 2026.

Generations of moviegoers were brought up on the Star Wars movies, and the franchise continues to expand thanks to live-action shows available with a Disney+ subscription. The sequel trilogy ended a few years ago, but there's still discourse surrounding Rian Johnson's subversive sequel The Last Jedi. The movie got some backlash, but would the filmmaker still return to the galaxy far, far away? Someone recently asked him.

When The Last Jedi hit theaters it was met with backlash from Star Wars fans, largely thanks to a number of unexpected plot twists. During a conversation with Variety, Johnson reflects on bringing his entry into the space opera to life, calling it "the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made.” He went on to share:

I felt just so connected to it, and just cared so deeply about every single element of it. I think especially with something that has a big cultural impact and belongs to everybody, that makes it even more important for you and the entire team to make it personal for yourselves, to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside of you.

Talk about a glowing review. Clearly the time away from the franchise hasn't quelled Rian Johnson's fond feelings for The Last Jedi. And while we never got his announced Star Wars trilogy, he stands by both the process and the final product that hit theaters back in 2017.

I personally love The Last Jedi, and think it's the most memorable entry in the sequel trilogy. I mean, Holdo's hyperspace ram is worth the price of admission alone. While Johnson stands by his work in the blockbuster, is he still willing to return to George Lucas' franchise? In the same interview he addressed this by saying:

I love ‘Star Wars’ more now than I ever have. And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now, taking cracks at it. I’m already writing the next thing I’m gonna do, and it’s not a ‘Star Wars’ thing or a ‘Knives Out’ thing. Right now, I’m very much enjoying making my own stuff, but if the opportunity presented itself, it’s a world I deeply love.

I'll take it. While not an all-out confirmation, Rian Johnson hasn't ruled out the possibility of returning for another Star Wars movie. The franchise has been away from the big screen for a few years, but that'll change in 2027 with Shawn Levy's Starfighter. Fingers crossed that the Knives Out filmmaker eventually gives it another spin in the beloved science-fiction property.

Star Wars will return to theaters when Shawn Levy's Starfighter hits theaters on May 28th as part of the 2027 movie release list. For now fans can re-watch all the movies (including The Last Jedi) over on Disney+.

#3445. Lazio, mercato di gennaio: i conti decidono tra via libera e blocco

La Commissione esaminerà i dati al 30 settembre; a Formello si teme uno stop, ma resta la possibilità di intervenire sui conti.

La Lazio attende l’esame dei conti al 30 settembre per sapere come potrà operare nel mercato di gennaio: liberamente, a saldo zero o con un blocco. Secondo quanto riportato da Calciomercato.it, A Formello prevale un leggero pessimismo e il club si aspetta lo stop, che potrebbe però essere superato con le misure previste dall’articolo 90 delle Noif.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

La Commissione che ha sostituito la Covisoc valuterà la documentazione presentata dalla società. Se la Lazio avrà raggiunto il parametro dello 0,70%, potrà muoversi liberamente. Se la situazione sarà peggiorata rispetto a marzo, il mercato sarà bloccato; negli altri casi, il club opererà a saldo zero.

La Lazio arriva da una sessione estiva a saldo zero. Al 31 marzo il rapporto tra costi e ricavi aveva superato la soglia dello 0,70%, raggiungendo lo 0,82%, con un disavanzo di circa 20 milioni di euro e un conseguente blocco parziale.

Nel recente bilancio, il costo del personale è salito da 98,2 a 104,6 milioni di euro e gli ammortamenti dei calciatori da 32,7 a 38,4 milioni. Il monte ingaggi è invece sceso da 79,5 a circa 75 milioni. Il club ha inoltre inserito a bilancio 7 milioni legati a Polymarket, limitati alla quota del primo anno dell’accordo quinquennale di sponsorizzazione, bloccato dall’autorità.

Incideranno anche gli incassi del botteghino e i mancati introiti europei. La scorsa stagione la Lazio aveva messo a bilancio circa 20 milioni dagli ingressi allo stadio; in quella attuale, lo sciopero del tifo ha bloccato questa entrata. In caso di stop al mercato, la società potrebbe pagare una sanzione e coprire l’eventuale deficit per rientrare nei parametri. Lotito sta cercando di sistemare il passivo inserendo crediti o dilazionando alcuni pagamenti, in particolare quelli relativi al periodo Covid.
