#3444. If You're Tired Of Colleen Hoover Movies, Watch This Overlooked 2026 Rom-Com

Colleen Hoover is the reigning queen of BookTok-phenomenon-turned-movie entertainment. The woman just has a knack for writing the kinds of books that might not get a lot of critical love but which social media crowds cannot resist. Thus far, that has resulted in four Colleen Hoover movie adaptations. Unfortunately, none of them are very good. At least, the critics didn't like them. Audiences, on the other hand, keep showing up. Following the less than enthusiastic response to the latest Hoover movie, "Verity," however, even fans might be in need of a break. In which case, might I suggest "You, Me & Tuscany," directed by Kat Coiro.

Corio previously helmed the 2022 glossy rom-com relic "Marry Me" starring Jennifer Lopez and Owen Wilson. Like your standard Hoover affair, it movie earned an okay 61% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, but managed to push the "popcornmeter" to 92%, meaning audiences absolutely loved Coiro's movie — which was based on a webcomic.

In 2026, Coiro — who also directed several episodes of "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law" — returned with another romantic comedy: "You, Me & Tuscany," an original story written by Ryan Engle, who, oddly enough, has mostly written actioners such as the Idris-Elba-vs.-a-lion survival horror "Beast" and the Liam Neeson outing that was 2014's "Non-Stop." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he embraced his more tender side with a story of a young cook who finds love in the titular Italian region.

"You, Me & Tuscany" stars Halle Bailey ("The Little Mermaid") as Anna, a young woman who after losing her house-sitting job, meets a strapping Italian named Matteo Costa (Lorenzo de Moor). Following their brief encounter, Anna decides to fly to Italy and manages to find a spare key to Matteo's empty Tuscan villa. There, Matteo's mother, Gabriella (Isabella Ferrari) arrives and Anna decides to lie and tell her that she's Matteo's fiancé.

It might seem as though "You, Me & Tuscany" is yet another fake dating rom-com, whereby a feigned romance becomes real. But the movie diverges from that well-worn path when Matteo's cousin, Michael (Regé-Jean Page) arrives and there's an instant attraction between he and Anna.

Page is, of course, best known for playing Simon Basset, the Duke of Hastings, in Season 1 of Netflix's hugely-popular series "Bridgerton." But he's since enjoyed a successful film career and is quickly making a name for himself in Hollywood. Page's Simon Basset left "Bridgerton" after the first season, after which the actor appeared in "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves," and in Steven Soderbergh's sleek spy thriller "Black Bag." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he further proved he has leading man chops. Otherwise, however, the movie doesn't do much to separate it from the glut of sort-of-okay romance movies with which we've been inundated in recent years. But it has at least outdone every Colleen Hoover movie on Rotten Tomatoes.

The latest Colleen Hoover movie was the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which no doubt left many viewers disappointed in the lack of straightforward romance. Much of the movie features Anne Hathaway glaring silently at Dakota Johnson from a medical bed or wheelchair. "You, Me and Tuscany" on the other hand should delight those hoping for more schmaltzy romance in the vein of Lili Reinhart's Prime Video smash hit "The Love Hypothesis" or Sofia Carson's similarly popular Netflix romance "My Oxford Year."

Over on Rotten Tomatoes, it's a familiar state of affairs. "You, Me & Tuscany" earned a somewhat respectable 65% critic score while managing to push the "popcornmeter" all the way to 91%. This is the rom-com pattern of late. Audiences clearly got what they came for here, even if Nikki Gemmell of The Australian called the movie "the filmic equivalent of paint by numbers, lift muzak, Fruit Loops, Contiki Tours and The Voice," essentially "anything that feels bland, inauthentic and deeply commercial." Sadly, this is just where we are in 2026. We used to make rom-coms like "Sleepless in Seattle" and "When Harry Met Sally." Not anymore.

"You, Me & Tuscany," however, isn't the worst example of the modern day rom-com (Netflix's "The Wrong Paris" might have claimed that title in 2025). If you happen to be looking for a Hoover palette cleanser that also isn't too far removed from the author's BookTok-friendly brand of romance, then this one's worth a go. "You, Me & Tuscany" is currently available to rent from the usual platforms, and can be streamed via Peacock with a premium subscription.

#3443. Leighton Meester's Christmas Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Former "Gossip Girl" star Leighton Meester is currently dominating the Netflix streaming charts with her latest movie. A now-famous actress whose career started on "Law & Order," she's come a long way over the years. To that end, Meester's "Guarding Stars" is now the biggest streaming hit on the biggest streaming service in the world.

Described as "a cozy, snowy Christmas rom-com," director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum's "Guarding Stars" is currently sitting in the number one spot on Netflix's most-watched movie charts, per FlixPatrol. The movie co-stars former "Supernatural" star Jared Padalecki. Since The CW canceled Padelecki's "Walker," he's had more time to focus on other stuff, such as this holiday flavored romantic comedy.

The movie centers on a no-nonsense bodyguard (Meester) who is assigned to protect a charming action star over the holidays. Sparks fly, secrets unravel, and Christmas gets a whole lot more complicated. The movie is inspired by the 2022 novel "The Bodyguard" by Katherine Center. The ensemble cast also includes Andie MacDowell ("Magic Mike XXL"), Noah LaLonde ("Deer Camp '86"), Toby Sandeman ("Running Point"), Rachael Ancheril ("Star Trek: Discovery"), Shaun Johnston ("Heartland"), pop star Ava Max, and country singer Walker Hayes in his acting debut.

Netflix wisely decided to drop this movie just before Thanksgiving. The holidays are kicking off and this is very much on point with the theme of the holiday. It's precisely the kind of thing people are looking to throw on while scrolling for something to watch. This sort of stuff thrives this time of year. As further evidence of that, the Colleen Hoover movie "Reminders of Him" was also recently Netflix's biggest streaming hit.

Rom-coms can still find success at the box office these days, with Glen Powell and Sydney Sweeney's "Anyone But You" serving as a fine example from recent history. But Netflix has really managed to dominate this space in recent years. They've made genuinely charming gems like "Always Be My Maybe," one of the best rom-coms on Netflix, and launched full-on franchises such as "The Kissing Booth."

But the king of the streamers has really thrived when it comes to romantic holiday fare. One of the most prominent examples was when 2024's strange Christmas movie "Hot Frosty" took over Netflix, becoming a genuine cultural sensation at the time. Admittedly, "Guarding Stars" is much more traditional than a movie in which a snowman comes to life. All the same, that almost makes its success more noteworthy, as it didn't have to rely on some goofy hook to get it across the finish line.

There's probably an element of this premise that seems cozy and fitting the spirit of the season, but pairing two former CW stars like Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki, especially with one in an against-type role as a bodyguard, appears to have intrigued viewers quite a bit.

The movie was written by Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith ("Isn't It Romantic," "Virgin River") alongside Gina Matthews and Grant Scharbo. Robin Fisichella served as the executive producer, with Matthews, Scharbo, Jared and Genevieve Padalecki on board as producers.

"Guarding Stars" is streaming now on Netflix.

When it was announced that Robert Pattinson had been cast as James Bond, Twilight fans everywhere did a little cheer. Especially if you were Team Edward! What a good long-term investment that’s turned out to be! However, the most popular Twilight-related reaction to Pattinson being 007 stems from the fact that the iconic spy was brought up in the vampire movie. As it turns out, there’s a whole new layer to that scene we didn’t know about.

First off, in case you missed it, James Bond is brought up around 58 minutes into 2008’s Twilight. Just seconds before Edward Cullen and Bella Swan make their grand entrance as a couple for the first time at school, one of their classmates, Eric, hands out flyers for the upcoming prom, which is a Monte Carlo theme. Check out the scene below:

Twilight literally predicted Robert Pattinson being James Bond btw https://t.co/eMfeaVhbhuNovember 16, 2026

Isn’t that wild? James Bond is literally said in Twilight right before the current James Bond appears. However, there’s more to it. The movie’s director, Catherine Hardwicke, revealed something new about the scene while talking about the casting on The Kyle Buchanan Show. In her words:

I said, ‘Let’s put the sunglasses on that day,’ and he got out of the car and he looked so suave that he inspired the line Bond, James Bond… Justin kind of ad-libbed it. It’s kind of cool because we did think he looked like James Bond. So, I guess we were seeing the future.

That happened 18 years before it became a reality. I guess it goes to show the role has been right for Robert Pattinson all along given those on the set of Twilight were thinking about it, too. Pattinson didn’t earn the role easily, either. All sorts of other eligible actors such as Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden reportedly auditioned for Denis Villeneuve’s film. Charlie Cox also recently said he was shot down for being “too old” even though he’s just three years older than Pattinson.

Hardwicke certainly had a hand in making Pattinson the big name he is. And, while talking about the actor, she recalled what stuck out about him when he auditioned for Twilight. In her words:

He’s intense, and he’s interesting, and he’s got a lot of stuff going on in there, and he’s weird and he’s original. He doesn’t fit the mold and he’s not scared to think or say crazy shit, which is what I love about him.

While it’s perhaps a bit surprising Amazon MGM Studios didn’t opt for an actor who was an unknown, Jeff Bezos has said that in the screen tests it was “so obvious” Pattinson was their Bond that they didn’t dare pick anyone else. We can’t wait to see what his Bond will be like, and given his career thus far, it sounds like it might be unexpected.

While we wait for Bond 26, you can get excited to see Robert Pattinson in Dune: Part 3 on December 18. Oh, and the whole Twilight saga is there for anyone with a Netflix subscription.

#3440. 12 Most Devastating Deaths In The Hunger Games Movies, Ranked

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the ReapingThe Hunger Games movies have some of the most devastating deaths in all of cinema. This includes the newly released Sunrise on The Reaping, which details Panem's second Quarter Quell and Haymitch's victory nearly 25 years before the events of the first Hunger Games movie with Katniss Everdeen.

Whether it's countless children being forced to fight to the death and/or those who choose to resist the Capitol, the Hunger Games franchise has delivered several truly heartbreaking moments. While this can come from the loss of characters who'd been developed over the course of several movies, even those with minimal screen time can still meet fates that are incredibly hard to watch.

When trying to determine the most tragic fate in the franchise, the list below considers the circumstances of each character's death, the emotional impact, and what the loss means for the franchise narrative at large. Keeping that in mind, here's our ranking of the 12 most heartbreaking deaths across all The Hunger Games movies and prequels, including Sunrise on the Reaping.

Wyatt Callow's death is one of the earliest tragedies in Sunrise on the Reaping once the 50th Hunger Games actually begin.

One of the four tributes chosen from District 12, Wyatt rushes to protect the younger Lou Lou and is quickly killed with an axe to the back from Silka, one of the vicious career tributes. This happened mere moments after the very start of the Games. While it may not be the most gruesome death in the franchise, it's truly heartbreaking to see Wyatt die so suddenly after all the time spent in the first act of the movie introducing him along with his fellow District 12 tributes.

Having been an Oddsmaker back in District 12, there's a cruel irony that the odds clearly weren't in Wyatt's favor the moment he himself was put into the Hunger Games.

The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes' Wovey is one of the youngest tributes in the 10th Hunger Games, making her death particularly hard to watch.

Representing District 8, Wovey held Lucy Gray's hand as they walked into the arena and hid for almost all of the games. She only came out when she heard the large Capitol drone overhead, thinking the Games were over. Instead, she was one of the first to be completely overwhelmed by the horde of venomous and genetically altered rainbow-colored snakes dropped into the arena. Having stood very little chance of actually surviving the Games beyond her ability to climb and hide, Wovey's death is easily one of the most heartbreaking in Songbirds and Snakes.

In the main Hunger Games series, Cinna is one of Katniss' most important allies. A fashion designer secretly supporting the ongoing rebellion against the Capitol, Cinna's designs for Katniss became symbols of resistance, culminating with the transformation of her wedding dress into a Mockingjay in Catching Fire, a moment that cemented Katniss as the ultimate symbol of rebellion.

As a result, Cinna is arrested and beaten by Capitol Peacekeepers just before she enters the arena for the third Quarter Quell. It wasn't until after Katniss was extracted by the rebellion and taken to District 13 that she would learn of Cinna's tragic off-screen death during interrogation. Nevertheless, seeing him beaten and dragged away toward an inevitable demise with Katniss helpless to intervene will always be one of the most brutal scenes in the core Hunger Games movies.

Ampert's death in Sunrise on the Reaping is especially cruel, as he's effectively marked for death well before the 50th Hunger Games even begin. This is because Ampert is the son of Beetee, a former victor. After Beetee was caught with plans to disrupt the Capitol's communications systems, his punishment was Ampert being reaped and Beetee being forced to mentor his own son.

Even so, Ampert still helped Haymitch during the Games with Beetee's plan to sabotage the arena. However, Ampert is ultimately attacked by a horde of vicious mutt squirrels, with Haymitch unable to save the young boy despite his best efforts. Not only is it one of the most horrifying mutt deaths, but it's a prime example highlighting the greater context of President Snow's endless cruelty.

Mags Flanagan's sacrifice during the second Quarter Quell is one of the most selfless and tragic moments in Catching Fire. When the poisonous fog threatens to envelop the unified tributes, the elderly Mags recognizes her inability to keep up with the others.

Mags was effectively a surrogate mother to Finnick Odair, having been his mentor when he was the youngest to ever win the Games. Mags also volunteered and took Annie Cresta's place during the uniqie victor's reaping for the 75th Hunger Games' Quarter Quell.

As such, Finnick was determined to save Mags and was carrying her on his back, just barely staying ahead of the toxic fog. However, Mags ends up willingly entering the fog after kissing Finnick goodbye. Removing herself from the board, Mags' sacrifice helped ensure that the younger tributes had better odds of survival.

Sejanus Plinth is one of the few characters in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes who recognizes the cruelty of the fairly new Hunger Games and wants to do something about the Capitol's treatment of the Districts. However, it's his compassion and decision to help District 12 rebels that makes him a major threat to the government, as well as to the ambitions of his best friend, young Coriolanus Snow.

After secretly recording Sejanus' intentions to help the rebellion, Snow betrays Sejanus and sends the evidence to the Capitol. This leads to Plinth's arrest and hanging, with jabberjays perfectly mimicking his cries to his mother after his death. Not only that, but Sejanus' father ends up treating Snow like a son and names him his heir for being "such a good friend" to his son, supporting his education and rise to power (never knowing the major hand Snow had in Sejanus' death), thereby making his demise that much more devastating.

While the deaths of his mother and brother in a fire were horrible, Lenore Dove's death is arguably the most brutal consequence of Haymitch's victory in the 50th Hunger Games, and one of the most devastating in either of The Hunger Games' prequel films.

Having completely destroyed Haymitch's life after the Games, Snow orchestrates the poisoning of gumdrops that were eaten by the love of Haymitch's life, having wrongly assumed the candies were from Haymitch himself. Helpless to do anything but watch Lenore Dove die in his arms, her death is the start of Haymitch's lifetime of grief and isolation, refusing to let anyone get close to him for fear that Snow would kill them next while constantly drinking in a desperate attempt to numb the pain and forget.

Maysilee Donner's death is easily one of the most emotionally devastating moments near the end of the 50th Hunger Games in Sunrise on the Reaping. Having joined Haymitch as two of the last tributes left standing, the two tributes from 12 had a genuine bond as allies and their shared determination to defy the Capitol. However, Maysilee was killed by a flock of flamingo-like bird mutts with razor-sharp beaks the novel confirms were designed to target her specifically and ignore Haymitch, yet another punishment from Snow to make him suffer.

With Maysilee being the third and final tribute to die in Haymitch's arms after Lou Lou and Ampert, the lengths Snow goes to punish Haymitch for his defiance of the Capitol can not be understated. Maysilee's death is particularly cruel, especially considering how it was shown via the Capitol's coverage, with careful editing and narration framing Haymitch as a selfish coward.

Maysilee's death is made even worse during her funeral back at District 12, with a traumatized Haymitch mistaking her twin sister Merrilee as Maysilee herself. Lastly, knowing that Katniss and Peeta later watch footage of her death and Haymitch's "victory" in Catching Fire makes her loss even more significant and impactful.

The youngest tribute from District 12 during Sunrise on the Reaping, it's incredibly tragic and cruel that 13-year-old Louella McCoy never even makes it to the Hunger Games' arena. Having been Haymitch's childhood friend from District 12, the duo promised to have each other's backs. However, the horses during the tributes' chariot parade were spooked by fireworks thrown from the audience. Mass mayhem ensued with Haymitch and Louella's chariot slamming into another. While Haymitch was thrown free, Louella was dragged under the flipped-over chariot before suffering a lethal head injury.

Carrying Louella's body to Snow, an angered Haymitch sarcastically applauds the debacle with a slow clap that effectively puts him in the President's crosshairs. However, what makes her death so much worse is that the Capitol refuses to even acknowledge it.

Shortly after the botched parade, Snow has Louella replaced with an abducted lookalike from District 11 who'd been traumatized and brainwashed to believe herself to be Louella, though the rest of the District 12 tributes chose to call her Lou Lou. On the whole, the Capitol erasing Louella's existence is arguably just as bad and even more disturbing than the death itself. To make matters worse, Haymitch fails to protect Lou Lou in the arena after she's poisoned by toxic flowers early on in the Games.

Without a doubt, Finnick Odair's Mockingjay death is one of the most shocking losses in the entire Hunger Games franchise. After surviving the 75th Hunger Games and becoming a key member of the rebellion at District 13, Finnick finally marries fellow victor Annie Cresta, one of the rare moments of happiness in the franchise's final Mockingjay films.

However, Finnick's future is brutally robbed during the mission to assassinate Snow when he falls into a horde of horrifying lizard-humanoid mutts after helping Katniss and the others escape the sewer tunnels below the Capitol. Katniss is then forced to detonate an explosive device to cover the rest of their team's escape and prevent the mutts from dragging away. Overall, there's a wide consensus that Finnick's death is one of the most devastating considering just how close he was to having his happy ending with Annie.​​​​​​​

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3439. Stranger Things Star Noah Schnapp Reveals Photo From Failed Hunger Games Audition For Haymitch

Now that he's free of "Stranger Things," we're going to find out if Noah Schnapp can fulfill the promise he flashed over five seasons of the Netflix sci-fi/horror series. His character, Will Byers, had arguably the most emotional arc of the show, with viewers watching him go from missing boy to psychically tortured returnee from the Upside Down to out and proud young adult. Byers' journey mirrored Schnapp's personal voyage to coming out of the closet in 2025. The "Hunger Games" prequel is currently tearing up the box office, so it would've been a sweet gig for the 22-year-old actor. But he congratulated Joseph Zada like a gentleman for landing the role, and, as an egoless bonus, the brunette Schnapp posted a still picture of himself in blonde hair from his screen test to Instagram. (See below.)

After a couple of ... emojis, Schnapp tagged Zada and added, "Think they picked right for this one."

I have no true measure of Noah Schnapp as an actor. He's handsome, he's got some mystery to him and, in the right role (e.g. Will Byers), he connects. Do I think he would've been an effective Haymitch Abernathy, given all the horrible things that happen to the character on his way to growing up and becoming Woody Harrelson? Maybe not.

"Affluenza" ended its London run on November 21, and, boy, did the critics lay into this sucker. In a one-star review for The Guardian, Arifa Akbar called it an "epic wreckage," adding, "You want to look away, for shame, but simply can't stop gawping." Most critics concurred, but that actually worked out for Schnapp, as they were too busy lambasting Sandberg to pay much attention to his performance. Writing for The Times, Clive Davis simply noted that Schnapp "doesn't disgrace himself." If you get cast in a disaster, you can live with that.

It's unclear where Schnapp will go from here, but thanks to "Stranger Things" he has a pretty sizable fan base. I can't see him being a part of the forthcoming series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure," which is a prequel set in the 1950s, but we'll certainly see more of him in the future.

#3437. This X-Men Character Is The One Marvel Hero Doctor Doom Respects The Most

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Doctor Victor von Doom's ego and conviction in his own superiority are as enormous as the universe, but in his cold heart, he does respect some of the "foolish" heroes who oppose him. Doom unconditionally loves his goddaughter, Valeria Richards of the Fantastic Four. He is frenemies with Namor the Sub-Mariner, and also maintains a friendly rivalry with his fellow sorcerer Doctor Stephen Strange; their dynamic lacks the bitterness that defines Doom's feud with Reed Richards. Doom also acknowledges Captain America as a paragon of his chosen ideals, and sees even Spider-Man's puerility as if he's a court jester, the one willing to tell a king what no one else will.

But there's one hero that Doom most consistently views and addresses as an equal, and that's Ororo Monroe, Storm, of the X-Men. Storm is easily one of the strongest X-Men; she can control the weather itself and is a self-styled "goddess." Even Doom concedes her that description. Unusually for Doom, he rarely tries to downplay Storm's power next to his own. Ororo's strength intrigues him — as does her beauty.

Now, Doom isn't the kind of man to act on romantic whimsy. "Doom needs no one" is one of his self-affirming catchphrases, and he once drove away his childhood sweetheart Valeria to prioritize his quest for knowledge and power. Part of Doom's self-inflicted misery is choosing to believe that no woman could ever love a man with a scarred face like his, yet another reason Doom hides behind a mask: "How could she... when even I am driven to madness by the sight!" But even so, one feels Doom would revel in the fantasy of Storm sitting by his side. It all goes back to their first meeting in "Uncanny X-Men" #145 by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum.

"Uncanny X-Men" issues #145-147 comprise a short arc where the twisted gamesman Arcade teams up with Doom to destroy the X-Men. In #145, Storm shows up at Doom's castle... and he welcomes her as an honored guest, treating her to a feast while the other X-Men are attacked by mecha-armored guards. Storm herself is charmed by Doom, thinking he is "a fascinating man," and he reciprocates.

"Storm seems drawn to me, as I am to her. Lioness to lion. Queen to king. She does not fear me. She should. She will."

Indeed, Doom soon defeats the X-Men, Storm included, as he dismisses them all as simple "children" next to him. While the others are thrown into deathtraps, Doom — charmed as he was by Storm — transmutes the still conscious Ororo into a chrome statue, while creating a robot in Storm's image to serve him. For Ororo, who is claustrophobic, being trapped inside her own body is a living hell. Once freed, she lives up to her name and unfurls a terrifying storm. Echoing Doom's own words, Storm declares: "Am I not beautiful, Lord Doom? And terrible? Do you not fear me? You should. You shall."

Normally, this would be a bungled first impression. But after surrendering Arcade, Doom apologizes to Storm for his behavior, suggesting his infatuation with her was real: "I would hope that we might begin anew. You are a fascinating woman. I should like to know you better." Ororo grants him the grace of a clean slate.

The events of this arc are referenced almost any time Doom and Storm meet, such as in issue #4 of Storm's 2024 solo series, where Doom hosts her in Latveria. He's not alone among villains in his view of Storm, either.

Read any of Chris Claremont's writing, including the hundreds of "X-Men" stories to his name, and it's easy to tell that he's got a thing for powerful women. No "X-Men" character more consistently shows that than Storm, the strongest of the team and their frequent leader. It often feels like Claremont wrote his own infatuation with the character into the text; "powerful villain tries to take Storm as theirs" is a stock Claremont "X-Men" plot, and not just with Doom.

Claremont and Bill Sienkiewicz's "Uncanny X-Men" #159 sees Dracula himself try to turn Storm into his bride. (New comic series "Midnight X-Men" takes place in a timeline where he succeeded, and Storm reigns as a vampire queen.)

An attraction to Storm binds Doom and Dracula... or does it? Shortly after Doom's guest appearance in "X-Men," writer-artist John Byrne took over "Fantastic Four." Byrne had made his name drawing "X-Men," but ultimately left due to creative differences with Claremont. A lingering mark of those differences shows up in "Fantastic Four" #258. Byrne, apparently dissatisfied with how Claremont wrote Doom, suggests the Doom who teamed up with Arcade was one of Doom's robotic duplicates, or Doombots.

Now, in the "X-Men" issues themselves, there's no hint this isn't the real Doom. Years later, in Al Ewing and Stefano Caselli's "S.W.O.R.D." #7, Storm hosts Doom for dinner, and their conversation is loaded with references to "X-Men" #145. Doom blames his unbecoming behavior of attacking Storm, his guest, as a Doombot's faulty programming (but he would, wouldn't he?). Across the conversation, Doom demonstrates his interest in Storm is all too real, to the point Ororo tells him: "Don't flirt, Victor. It's unbecoming." Except, Doom would likely argue, with an exceptional woman like her.

#3436. Guy Pearce's Gory '90s Horror Western Movie Deserved Better At The Box Office

One of the enduring American monster myths is the Wendigo or the forest spirit that possesses and compels men to become cannibals. Originally a myth of the Algonquian peoples, the Wendigo has become a monster of comic books, horror films, and more, like Stephen King's chilling novel "Pet Sematary."

Possibly the strangest Wendigo movie is the 1999 horror western comedy "Ravenous," inspired by real tales of 19th century cannibalism on the frontier like the Donner Party. During the Mexican–American War, Lieutenant John Boyd (Guy Pearce) plays dead during battle. Hidden among a cart of deceased soldiers, Boyd takes an enemy fort. A hero but also a coward, Boyd is then reassigned to a remote outpost in the Sierra Nevada mountains.

Curiously, during Boyd's seizure of the fort, he seemed to gain strength when the blood of the dead dripped down onto his tongue. In that moment, Boyd became an unknowing Wendigo, acquiring the strength of the men whose blood he drank — and he's not the only one on the mountain. A traveler named F.W. Colqhoun (Robert Carlyle) shows up at the fort, claiming to be the survivor of a band of wagon travelers killed and cannibalized by their guide, one Colonel Ives. But "Colqhoun" is Ives and, seizing control of the camp, plots to turn it into a cannibal colony. He recognizes Boyd as a seeming kindred spirit, and the movie becomes a test of whether Boyd will succumb to Ives' pressure and his own Wendigo hunger.

"Ravenous" was a box office bomb in its day, grossing $2 million against a $12 million budget, and it received largely underwhelmed or confounded reviews. But don't take that as a mark against the movie, which has a following to this day. (Any "Yellowjackets" fan should make watching "Ravenous" a priority.)

For "Ravenous" to work, Boyd's temptation needs to feel real. When you've got someone as charismatic as Robert Carlyle playing Ives, it sure does. That performance isn't the only way that Carlyle saved the movie.

"Ravenous" had a tumultuous production, and Guy Pearce has called "Ravenous" his worst experience shooting a movie. The film's original director Milcho Manchevski was fired mid-filming with 20th Century Fox moving to replace him with "Home Alone 3" director Raja Gosnell. The cast rejected that, and so Carlyle brought in director Antonia Bird, who he'd worked with on the 1997 crime film "Face." Bird is the credited director of "Ravenous," but was she able to wrangle the mess she'd inherited?

Even a "Ravenous" fan will admit the movie is, tonally, all over the place. After a scene of Ives revealing his true murderous self, the movie breaks out into a chase scene with comical banjo music. If you'll pardon the pun, "Ravenous" bites off a lot and tests how much it's capable of chewing. But that strangeness is a strength, as there's no other movie quite like "Ravenous."

In a 2015 retrospective review for Rolling Stone, critic David Ehrlich showed the kind of praise that has earned "Ravenous" a fanbase. Ehrlich complimented its unique tonal recipe and how, through its setting, it equates manifest destiny colonialism with literal cannibalism... while conceding those qualities are likely what turned off audiences in 1999.

Considering the 1990s saw Anthony Hopkins make Hannibal Lecter into a cinematic icon on the heels "The Silence of the Lambs," I can see why studio execs would invest in cannibal horror. But "Ravenous" was just too weird a movie to ever be a massive hit, even though it's found its supporters with time.

#3433. Chris Evans Reveals Whether Avengers: Doomsday Shows Doctor Doom's Face Under The Mask

Marvel Studios certainly made an impression, for good or ill, when it announced at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that Robert Downey Jr. would be returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe... but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man. Marvel fans instantly assumed, with good reason, that Doom was being reimagined as having some connection to Iron Man (i.e. that Victor von Doom would be a Tony Stark variant turned evil).

But surprisingly, the marketing for "Avengers: Doomsday" has not been leaning on any connection between Doom and Iron Man. The second "Doomsday" trailer confirms that he comes from the Fantastic Four's universe, Earth-828, and shares a history with them. The closest thing has been a new post-credits scene from "Avengers Endgame: Encore" that shows Doom forging his mask in a way mirroring Tony doing so back in 2008's "Iron Man." Speaking to Empire, Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige also stressed that, despite the double casting, RDJ's Doom is indeed Victor von Doom and not a Tony Stark variant.

Now, there is an easy out here. Doom is famous for wearing a metal mask to hide his supposedly scarred face. In the comics, he almost never takes that mask off. If it wanted, Marvel Studios could keep Doom in the mask and make it so him sharing an actor with Tony Stark becomes a non-issue. In fact, Chris Evans told Empire that's exactly what happens in "Doomsday," explaining:

"[Doom is] wearing a mask the whole time. That's not an easy challenge, to try and get your message across and be emotionally available to connect with. It just reinforces what I've always felt: Downey can do anything."

It feels pretty implausible Marvel would hire RDJ like this and not take full advantage of him, but I want to believe it.

When "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo announced Robert Downey Jr. as Doom on the SDCC stage, they said they felt they needed the "greatest actor in the world" to play the villain. Chris Evans' words to Empire echo that narrative: Downey is Doom only because he's the best actor for the part.

And in a vacuum, sure, yes, there's little doubt he can pull it off. During his MCU hiatus, RDJ won an Oscar for his turn in Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" as Lewis Strauss, who destroys J. Robert Oppenheimer's (Cillian Murphy) life out of a petty, misplaced grudge. Strauss is to "Oppie" as Doom is to Reed Richards!

But when you bring back your franchise's biggest star in a different role? And as part of a story that's all about different versions of characters from different universes colliding? Yeah, you can't blame people for assuming there's going to be an in-universe reason for Stark and Doom sharing a face.

This is pure speculation, but one going theory in Marvel fan communities is that Downey's casting as Doom is a smokescreen to hide that he'll also be returning as Iron Man in "Avengers: Secret Wars" (i.e. there's no need to hide him on the "Secret Wars" set because everyone will already know he's there playing Doom). You could pull that off if Doom indeed wears his mask the entire time, so the films don't present him and Stark as twins, and that bypasses the issue of RDJ getting no facetime if Doom keeps his mask on. I'll admit this appeals to me because it keeps Doom and Stark separate, which has always been my preference. But again, no clue if that's even remotely true.

It's worth noting that Chris Evans is also only talking about "Avengers: Doomsday." Perhaps that film will have Doom keep his mask on the whole time, and then only in "Secret Wars" will Doom be unmasked. There's some narrative sense to that: Part one of this story builds up Doom's threat, and then once he's won, you can explore the man underneath. In the original 1984 "Secret Wars" comics, after Doom steals the power of the godlike Beyonder, he uses it to heal his scarred face.

An adaptation of that scene practically writes itself. Doom, revealing his new power, unlatches his mask and shows himself free of any scarring. But this time, some of the heroes recognize Doom's face as Tony Stark's, and that opens up a mystery of why they look identical.

For what it's worth, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby always maintained Doom's face being "horribly scarred" was an exaggeration. No, Doom actually only has a small scar on his chin, but he's such an insecure egotist that he can't stand to let anyone — even himself — see that reminder of his imperfections, no matter how small they are. That's my preferred interpretation of comics Doom, but I'm not convinced crowded, multiverse-shattering blockbuster movies like "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars" will have room for that sort of psychological nuance.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is scheduled for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

#3432. GTA 6's Most Heartbreaking Scene Is Exactly Why You Had To Do All Those Chores

I was not ready to get so emotional over a coffee table

Grand Theft Auto 6 features as much shootin’, stealin’, and drug runnin’ as you’d expect from the latest entry in a series named after a felony. However, some players have been caught off-guard by just how much the early game is all about the more mundane parts of life. Namely, you gotta do a bunch of chores around the house. In many ways, GTA 6 is as much of an everyday life sim as it is a game about committing crimes.

Jason repairs the steps leading up to his and Lucia’s home, fixes a railing, buys groceries, orders flowers, paints the walls of their bedroom, and more to prepare for Lucia’s arrival from prison. All those chores might seem less thrilling than the opening hours you’d expect in a big-budget action game. But it turns out they set up a tragic heartbreak I simply did not see coming.

[Ed. note: Spoilers for the ending of Chapter 1 follow.]

Chapter 1 involves Jason and Lucia trying to get work from Mattia, the shady boyfriend of Kat, a mother-to-be whom Lucia befriended in prison. Part of that involves a standout sequence set to a Carly Rae Jepsen banger before Lucia gets lost in orgy central. (Vice City, y’all!) Bro, Mattia promises a job that could pay ten grand, bro. They just have to grab a bag from a locker and deliver it, bro.

Red flags abound, but Jason and Lucia go along for the ride, which quickly results in their arrest. Crooked cops show up, the couple gets into a shootout, and Jason gets grievously wounded while the couple struggle to keep hold over a bag containing who knows what.

GTA 6 does a great job of showing how various systems, both governmental and societal, are against Jason and Lucia, and that shines through here. In Jason and Lucia, Mattia sees a pair of not prospective partners, but a down-on-their-luck couple he can easily exploit — and they’re all too willing to play into his hands. Mattia leverages their desperation, even making them play dress up with Lucia in a platinum blonde wig and Jason in one of Mattia’s gaudy shirts, so they’d take the fall for whatever shady shit Mattia is up to. Clearly, he knew the danger surrounding this bag with shady cops and an organized outfit after it and gladly fed Jason and Lucia to the wolves.

They escape, but their horrible night has only just begun. Lucia takes Jason to his friend Cal, who brings Jason — and the mysterious bag — to the hospital. (Lucia later learns the hospital took everything from the couple’s BuckMe checking account as payment. America!) Lucia heads home to recover Jason’s stash, and tragedy strikes.

Upon entering their home, Lucia is jumped by masked criminals searching for that bag. Suddenly, the home Jason and Lucia built is now the arena for Lucia’s fight for her life. Flames engulf the sliding glass door that led to a patio where Jason would work out and the couple would hold one another while sipping their coffee and enjoying the morning sun. Those relaxing mornings are no more.

Tommy’s future crib that Jason bought during his video game night with Cal? Destroyed. A goon even tosses Lucia into it at one point, adding insult to injury. Where Tommy would have slept soundlessly — with a giant stuffed teddy in the corner — is now burning up. Also burning up is the hope that Jason and Lucia will get to live a normal life with Tommy, which the crib represented. Maybe in another life Jason and Lucia would have told Mattia to eat shit, bro, stayed patient, and welcomed Tommy to their little house on stilts in due time. Not in this life, however.

Watching the coffee table get destroyed hurt even more. Building furniture together with a shaky hex key is a quintessential couples activity, and Jason and Lucia do just that during a cute sequence earlier in the game. And then one of the masked men slams Lucia on it, shattering its glass top as their home continues to burn.

Flames raged after I dispatched those enemies. Still, I tried to have Lucia grab the stash from their burning bedroom, only to see her immediately get burned. (She’s fine.) I didn’t want the stash for the money, but the memories.

In Jason’s metal box, he has polaroid pictures showing him as a baby in his mother’s arms, him in football pads with his best friends, him with Lucia, and him with his army buddies. Jason’s a pretty stoic guy, so I wouldn’t expect him to outright say what these artifacts mean to him, but him keeping them alongside his rainy day fund says all it needs to. But, just like the crib, coffee table, and everything else, they’re gone. At least I was able to save the photo of Tommy, but not before screaming at my TV thinking I had missed it.

The house going up in flames is tragic on so many levels. It represented stability for the pair, a stability that they no longer have while trying to survive out of a crappy motel in Chapter 2’s Port Gellhorn. Not only did Jason spend his time fixing it up, but I spent my time fixing it up. I was immediately invested in that home as a result of the work I put into it. Now, it’s a pile of ash.

Everyone whining about the beginning segment of GTA 6 (how dare a game starring a romantic couple have an optional mission for the boyfriend to buy his girlfriend a necklace) missed the forest for the trees. Not only are the activities building a relationship between Jason and Lucia, but between the player and their controllable avatars. I’m over 20% into the story now, and I’ve already come to care for these two knuckleheads in the same way I care for characters in a BioWare game or my Baldur’s Gate 3 companions.

Rockstar’s GTA 6 has taken me by surprise every step of the way with how strong its writing is. I was a bit trepidatious going into it. Could any one game live up to years of massive hype, especially the highest-rated game ever? With its spotlight on two complex lead characters just trying to make it another day in a messed-up world, it’s delivered in spades. At the very least, no other game has made me care about a goddamn coffee table like GTA 6 has.

In my defense, I don’t know how to drive IRL or in GTA

#3431. Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday Might Have The Biggest Box Office Opening Weekend Ever

There has been much discussion as to whether or not the Marvel Cinematic Universe has lost its lustre in recent years. Indeed, Marvel's 2025 box office proved the MCU has fallen from grace, at least in terms of launching newer or less surefire franchises. However, "The Avengers" remains a gold standard for audiences around the world, and "Avengers: Doomsday" is going to prove that in a big way In December. So much so that we could be looking at, quite literally, the biggest opening weekend of all time.

Directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, aka the Russo Brothers, "Doomsday" is currently expected to open with a whopping $375 to $424 million domestically on the weekend of December 18, per Box Office Theory. Mind you, that's just in North America, not worldwide. If this pans out, even on the low end, it would set a new high bar for cinema, financially speaking. "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ruled the box office back in July with a record $360 million domestic debut, yet "Doomsday" looks like it might clear that with ease.

Even more surprising? The latest "Avengers" film is opening directly against the much-anticipated "Dune: Part Three," which is eyeing a blockbuster debut in the $91 to $115 million range. As a result, the so-called cinematic double bill known as Dunesday will blow Barbenheimer out of the water at the box office.

The latest "Avengers" cinematic event follows beloved heroes from three distinct universes as they're set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they've ever encountered. Namely, Doctor Doom, played by former "Iron Man" star Robert Downey Jr. The Russos previously helmed both "Avengers: Infinity War" and "Avengers: Endgame," which also bodes well.

"Avengers: Doomsday" trailers are selling the film as the MCU's biggest event yet, and, much like "Infinity War" did in 2018, it's teeing up something even bigger. Specifically, "Avengers: Secret Wars," which will close out the MCU's Multiverse Saga by adapting one of the most beloved Marvel Comics storylines of all time.

It can't be emphasized just how staggering these numbers are. "Avengers: Endgame" smashed box office records with a $1.2 billion global opening in 2019, with its $357.1 million domestic figure serving as the opening weekend record until "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" came along. "Avengers: Endgame" also passed "Avatar" to reclaim the highest-grossing movie title earlier this year thanks to the "Encore" re-release. Its lifetime total sits at $2.94 billion worldwide.

In light of how up and down things have been for the MCU in recent years, there was doubt as to whether or not "Doomsday" could live up to sky high expectations. Evidently, audiences are still very interested in seeing Earth's Mightiest Heroes, despite anything else that's happened in the 2020s. It doesn't matter that "The Marvels" finished its box office run as the lowest-grossing MCU movie ever or that films like "Thunderbolts*" fell way short of commercial expectations. This is the Avengers.

Even more amazing is the fact that Disney and Marvel Studios are doing this without the benefit of IMAX screens. "Dune: Part Three" has those locked up, which is significant since IMAX has proved it's more important to the box office than ever before. But the Avengers don't need IMAX. Would it be nice? Sure, but they're going to shatter records either way.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3430. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Has A Unique Credit You Rarely See In Movies

Suzanne Collins is the engine that drives the "Hunger Games" franchise. As the author behind the books, none of the movies happen without her. Beyond that, though, Collins has remained very close to the adaptations of her work, with Lionsgate consulting with her every step of the way. That's especially true with the franchise's latest prequel film, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" — so much so that it resulted in a unique credit we rarely see in movies.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" ruled the box office on its opening weekend, meaning that quite a few people might have noticed that once the credits roll, there's some text reading, "Adaptation by Suzanne Collins." So, while Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie are credited with the movie's screenplay, Collins got credit for the adaptation of her 2024 book of the same name. This is exceptionally rare in Hollywood.

"In the interest of avoiding a multiplicity of credits, the Guild is opposed to the general use of the 'Adaptation by' credit," the Writers Guild of America's screen credits manual states. But that doesn't mean it never gets used, and "Sunrise on the Reaping" warranted its rare usage. The manual further explains:

"The Guild recognizes that there are certain unusual cases where credit is due a writer who shapes the direction of screenplay construction without qualifying for 'Screenplay by' credit. In those special cases, and only as a result of arbitration, the 'Adaptation by' credit may be used."

Who gets credit for a screenplay can be difficult to actually pin down. In the movie business, it's rare that it's literally just one person writing a script and that's that. It's why Joss Whedon wasn't credited for his writing work on "Speed." It's also why Collins nabbed this unique credit.

Arbitration is a process used primarily to determine writing credits. As the WGA manual states, arbitration is usually the only way that this "Adaptation by" credit winds up being used. That doesn't mean that things got contentious between Billy Ray, Michael Lesslie, and Suzanne Collins, it's just a unique situation.

Collins generally feels happy with the "Hunger Games" movie adaptations and even co-wrote the first movie personally. By all accounts, she has a good relationship with Lionsgate, director Francis Lawrence, and other key creatives. The fact that she wound up with this rare credit, if anything, reflects her level of involvement.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, Ray offered a window into the collaboration, explaining that he communicated very directly with Collins when it came to determining how to adapt her latest book for the screen:

"At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, 'What is this book about for you?' She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume, and John Locke. And I said, 'Suzanne, what's the book about for you emotionally?' She said, 'It's about love and loss.' I said, 'Great, that's what I'm writing.' So, anything that didn't stick to that had to go."

In many cases, the writer of a book is left out in the cold when it comes to that book being turned into a movie. But not in this case. The few changes "Sunrise on the Reaping" makes to its source material don't appear to be against Collins' wishes. She was being consulted behind the scenes the whole way and was credited as such.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

#3429. Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Plan His Stunts

It’s a spectacular time to be a grifter. Basic truths keep getting harder for people to agree on, marketing is more dependent on hackable algorithms than traditional gatekeepers, and it seems like everyone is willing to uncritically listen to anyone offering them a shortcut. As Oobah Butler puts it in the first episode of his new HBO series “Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” we’re living through a “gold rush of bullshit.”

If that’s the case, Butler is a prospector who hits a paystreak everywhere he looks. After beginning his career as a musician, the British performance artist has devoted much of his past decade to the art of the scam. In 2017, he made headlines for creating a TripAdvisor profile for a nonexistent restaurant that briefly became the highest-rated eatery in London. His penchant for scams has only grown since then, culminating in “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.” The five-episode, “Nathan for You”-esque series sees him grift his way to the top of some of the slimiest industries on the planet including wellness supplements, wine, and dating apps with an approach that blurs the line between satire and how-to guides. Related Stories Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

When we spoke over Zoom, it was the first time I had ever interviewed a scammer. I naturally had to ask Butler if that was his preferred term (he had no problem with it), and how he would characterize his own unorthodox line of work.

“I think it sits somewhere between gonzo journalism and comedy. And I think we’re in a moment, in a culture, that’s just so rife with inauthenticity and scamming,” Butler said, explaining that just watching run-of-the-mill advertisements on a streaming service are enough to convince you that we live in an insane world. “One in three [ads] are AI now. And I don’t know why, that stuck in my mind recently where I was like, ‘Wow, these aren’t real people trying to sell me a product. They’re like prompts in a machine.’ So it’s an interesting line of work, but I think it feels very now, to be honest.”

The series should be essential viewing for anyone who either wants to laugh at the state of our seemingly elite spaces or just wants to make a quick buck in a dirty industry. Episodes illustrate how ecosystems of influencers and online ratings can be easily manipulated in pursuit of accomplishing ludicrous goals, like turning an undrinkable bottle of smoke tainted cabernet into one of Napa’s highest-rated wines of the year or marketing a skincare product as “endorsed by Cameron Diaz” because a random Hispanic guy was willing to slap his name on it for $50.

It’s a funny enough premise, but Oobah and his small team (which included frequent Safdie collaborator Ronald Bronstein) found that their best laid plans left them insufficiently prepared for the greed and stupidity that they’d encounter in the real world. The first episode begins with a scheme to market a new skin serum that’s allegedly made from the tears of small children. They thought that ridiculous idea could serve as the climax of an episode, but they soon found that the grifters they encountered had little issue with the idea — some of them even thought they could make money on it with the right tear-shaped bottle. The joke remained in the show, but it had to be reduced to a starting point before the episode devolved into crazier plans.

“We had a tip from a journalist that dermatologists can be full of shit and that they often can take money in exchange for recommendations. So we set up a lab where I had these kid actors with goggles on with tubes coming off them, and it was like we were milking the kids for the tears or whatever. We were like, ‘Right, we’re going to invite this dermatologist down here,’ a high-end Manhattan dermatologist, and we expected the dermatologist to laugh us out of the room,” he said. “What we couldn’t plan for doing that stunt is that the dermatologist would be like, ‘Awesome. Yeah, this is cool. Yeah, all right, interesting product. Maybe we could keep on working together, but I expect an endorsement fee.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh, you don’t give a fucking shit. You don’t care.'”

The incident cuts to the central problem of a show like this: it’s hard for satire to keep up with a world that only seems to get crazier every day. But Butler is not shying away from the challenge. He works quickly (the show began shooting this spring and wrapped in October before premiering on November 22), and is willing to change his plans whenever it turns out that a sincere actor has beaten him to one of his comedic scams. He already has plenty of ideas for a hypothetical Season 2, including taking on the recent trend of hotels and vacation rentals using AI-generated images that look nothing like their actual rooms. But the one thing he can count on is that the bullshit gold rush is not going to end any time soon.

“It’s hard to satirize something that’s so insane and fucked up,” he said. “That’s why in the first episode, we go and make a new product because it felt like the children’s tears thing wasn’t crazy enough. You know what I mean? So I literally go and make a human meat supplement, a lab-grown human meat supplement, and we go to this lab in Austin, we take stem cells from my stomach, we grow it over months and we create this thing. Because the actual reason we did that was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think children’s tears is scary because influencers would promote that.’ So I suppose that the crazier things get, the crazier the satire has to be able for it to be effective.”

“Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” airs Sunday nights on HBO at 11 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on HBO Max.

#3428. Why Joey From The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Looks So Familiar

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" brings back Brad Pitt as the stuntman from Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood." But he's the only major character returning for another round. That means David Fincher's follow-up with a script from Tarantino himself introduces a new ensemble of key characters, and one of them will instantly feel familiar in the film's opening sequence.

Without giving away any specific details of the flick, the Cliff Booth movie that critics are loving begins with Brad Pitt's character taking care of his duties as an employee at the New Beverly Cinema, a real-life Los Angeles movie-house that's now owned by Quentin Tarantino (though the theater in the movie is actually the Highland Theatre, owned by "Twilight" saga star Kristen Stewart). Booth keeps an eye on the film reels, refills the RC Cola syrup tank in the soda fountain, and closes up the theater when the credits roll on "Soul Brothers Die Hard!"

But once the theater is closed, that's when Booth's more pressing business begins. Two men who have been waiting in a car around the corner for the theater to closer show up with a bag, and they're making some kind of exchange for cash. One of the men might be recognizable to you, and that's Joey, played by Corey Fogelmanis. If you couldn't place who that actor was, but he looked familiar, this is where you might have seen him before.

Corey Fogelmanis most famous role might be that of the supporting character Farkle in the "Boy Meets World" spin-off/sequel series "Girl Meets World" on the Disney Channel. The series followed Riley (Rowan Blanchard), the daughter of Corey (Ben Savage) and Topanga (Danielle Fishel) from "Boy Meets World," as she navigates adolescent life, with many of the "Boy Meets World" cast members returning. By her side was her best friend Maya, played by none other than chart-topping pop star Sabrina Carpenter.

One of their other peers throughout the series was Farkle, a peculiar, nerdy character reminiscent of the character Minkus from "Boy Meets World," played by Lee Norris. Often used for comic relief, Farkle was a regular cast member on the series.

Since then, Fogelmanis has grown up considerably, and you might have seen him as a much different kind of teen in the horror movie "Ma" with Octavia Spencer. He continued to dabble in horror with a role in the Hulu Halloween movie "Carved," but he also showed his dramatic side as the lead of the coming-of-age drama "I Wish You All the Best."

Most recently, you've likely seen Fogelmanis as one of the titular characters in the Prime Video series "My Life with the Walter Boys." The series follows teenager Jackie Howard (Nikki Rodriguez) after a tragic accident forces her to leave her home and live with a guardian family who has nine brothers and a sister. Fogelmanis plays Nathan, one of the Walter brothers in the series, in almost all of the episodes.

Fogelmanis is still evolving and growing as an actor, and his role in the Cliff Booth movie will hopefully elevate his profile as a performer. Without spoiling anything, Fogelmanis' performance gives him a chance to show a bit of a darker side. There's also a bit of comedy in there too, albeit in a twisted fashion that only Fincher and Tarantino can deliver.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" hits IMAX theaters for just two weeks starting on November 25, 2026 before hitting Netflix on December 23.

#3426. 7 Funniest MST3K Episodes to Watch For Your Personal Turkey Day Marathon

We gather together to watch cheesy movies

Mystery Science Theater 3000 fans have always had a special relationship with American Thanksgiving. The show originally premiered on Thanksgiving Day in 1988, back in its public access era on KTMA TV in Minneapolis. Three years later, Comedy Central ran the first "Turkey Day" MST3K marathon, as both an anniversary celebration for the show and a 30-hour Thanksgiving special.

The Turkey Day tradition got dropped when MST3K moved from Comedy Central to the Sci-Fi Channel in 1997. (While Sci-Fi did run a MST3K marathon on Thanksgiving 1997, it wasn't labeled "Turkey Day.") That was the end of the tradition until 2013, when MST3K’s DVD distributor Shout! Factory revived Turkey Day via livestream.

2026's Turkey Day celebration, Back in Orbit, features six episodes from the Sci-Fi Channel run, as introduced by Mike Nelson, Kevin Murphy, and Bill Corbett. This is both a nod to their time as the hosts of the show during its Sci-Fi Channel run and a tie-in to the recently concluded MST3K/Rifftrax crossover spinoff, The Rifftrax Experiments.

This year's Turkey Day starts on Nov. 26 at noon EST on the official MST3K YouTube and Twitch channels, and is currently scheduled to feature:

That's a solid lineup of late-season MST3K. However, if you're interested in alternative programming (or you simply want a marathon on a day other than American Thanksgiving this year), just about all of the first 10 seasons of MST3K can be found for free on YouTube, either from old fan uploads or via the official MST3K channel. Due to MST3K's famous "keep circulating the tapes" mantra, the old uploads are the next best thing to officially endorsed, so you can binge guilt-free. Here are some more MST3K episodes to consider for your own Thanksgiving entertainment, sorted by their original broadcast order.

“I’m the luckiest boy in the world! I have slipped the surly bonds of Earth and touched the hand of God!”

MST3K really hit its stride in season 3. There are a few good episodes in the first two seasons, such as Catalina Caper and Robot Monster, but season 3 features a stacked roster of series-defining classics, and it starts with this hastily-made Italian fantasy film.

Cave Dwellers is a rebrand of the second movie in a four-part franchise starring the fantasy hero Ator (Miles O'Keefe). There's this whole rich vein of cheap B-movie sword-and-sorcery films from the mid-to-late 1980s that were all trying to cash in on the success of Arnold Schwarzenegger's Conan the Barbarian, and most of them are Italian knock-offs that were made in a week. The best of them are dumb fun; the worst are cocaine-infused unwatchable dreck.

What sets Cave Dwellers apart from the pack is that it takes some really big swings. It feels like one big continuity error even before the climactic moment where Ator instantly and inexplicably invents both hand grenades and the hang glider. It's a nearly perfect bad movie, both in its own right and as fodder for an MST3K episode.

“Hey, what gives? I’m on the milk carton.”

This was the episode that made MST3K click for me. Any B-movie fan knows there's a world of difference between "fun bad" and simply bad, and Pod People is about as fun-bad as it gets.

The backstory is reportedly that Spanish director Juan Piquer Simón (Pieces) set out to make a straightforward horror movie about a vacationing pop band that stumbles across a murderous alien. Then E.T. got popular, so Simón's producers demanded a reshoot to include an additional subplot about a boy who befriends an alien child.

The result was released in France and Spain as 1983's Extra Terrestrial Visitors, before being retitled to The Unearthling and Pod People for overseas release. It's a baffling mixture of at least three major plotlines, stitched together with little care for the final product. One moment is a heartwarming story of a child and his plush marketable alien pal; the next is some dude in a fursuit killing his way through a set of backup singers. That tonal mismatch makes Pod People a nearly perfect target for MST3K, which led to several of the show's most famous jokes.

“Every frame of this movie looks like someone’s last known photograph.”

To no one's real surprise, Manos is still generally considered the best episode of MST3K's run on Comedy Central, if not the single best episode. There are other good episodes in the fourth season, like City Limits and Hercules Unchained, but Manos overshadows them all. Like Pod People, this episode dug a notorious dud out of the back alleys of cinematic history and turned it most of the way into comedy gold.

I only say "most of the way" because Manos is a rough watch, even with Joel and the bots running interference. It's a truly baffling independent horror film from 1966, made with faulty equipment on a shoestring budget by a fertilizer salesman who allegedly did it all to win a bet. Manos is just so damn weird that it’s difficult to sit through. It was only ever screened at a handful of theaters in Texas before it appeared on MST3K, at which point it instantly became a legend.

Every frame of Manos is simply uncomfortable. The cast and crew of MST3K were always quite clear in behind-the-scenes featurettes that by the time they sat down to film an episode of the show, they'd watched the entirety of that episode’s featured movie at least five times. Despite that, Joel and the bots still manage to come off as realistically flabbergasted by each bizarre twist in Manos. There's a distinct point at which it stops being a classic MST3K episode and becomes pure trainwreck syndrome, whether you’ve seen the movie before or not.

Much like how Cave Dwellers is a reaction to the success of Conan the Barbarian, Escape 2000 (originally released as Escape From the Bronx, and not to be confused with the 1982 Australian humans-hunting-humans film) is an Italian clone of the first two Mad Max movies. It's set in a dystopian near-future New York City, as the gangs of the Bronx team up to defend their borough from a mega-corporation that wants to destroy and rebuild it. Come to think of it, Escape 2000 predicted gentrification.

Escape 2000 isn't actually that bad of a film. It's just cheaply made, overwrought, and has the same low-quality English dub as a lot of other '80s Italian B-movies, so if you’ve got a taste for that sort of thing you can have a good time with it. That makes it a solid target for the MST3K crew, which instantly lock in on a half-dozen running jokes in the first 10 minutes. It's hard to hear the word "Bronx" after this episode and not immediately think, "None of this would have happened if they'd just left the Bronx."

The first 10 seasons of MST3K were filmed in Minnesota, which neatly explains why the show was always so comfortable poking fun at Canadians. With that in mind, The Final Sacrifice is one long joke at Canada's expense, even before Mike and the bots sit down.

In another example of MST3K pulling a movie out of obscurity, 1990's The Final Sacrifice was made by a film student in Alberta on a budget of CA$1,500. Apparently it aired a few times on Canadian television in the early '90s, but was virtually unknown outside the country until its MST3K appearance.

The saving grace of The Final Sacrifice, both as a film and as an MST3K episode, is Zap Rowsdower (Bruce J. Mitchell). He might have the dumbest name of any character in film history, he's the sidekick until he's suddenly the hero in the last act, and he's a big buttery beer-fed ball of Canadian stereotypes. In other words, he's perfect. No notes. In a more perfect universe than this, Rowsdower would be on his tenth major motion picture, as he fights and drinks his way through unexplored Canadian action history. It's easily the highlight of this year's Turkey Day celebration, as it was hard to find online until recently, and it's worth incorporating into your own custom marathon.

”Why is he so impossible to hit? How can they keep missing this slow, giant white thing?”

Space Mutiny is still perhaps the most quotable episode of MST3K, even 29 years after it aired. It's given the internet decades of running jokes and forum handles, all at the expense of famous chunkhead Blast Hardcheese Punch Rockgroin Dave Ryder (Reb Brown, Yor, the Hunter From the Future) and his battle to save a colony ship from mutineers.

The co-stars of Space Mutiny have insisted since its release that it was meant to be a campy spoof of science fiction, but that's obviously damage control. Instead, it's obviously a million-dollar script paired with a buck-fifty budget. At its best, Space Mutiny is funny for all the wrong reasons, from Reb Brown’s random screaming to every woman on the colony ship wearing exercise gear as a “uniform” to the space battles that consist of visibly recycled footage from the original Battlestar Galactica. Its MST3K episode is one of the best in the series' run, often held up as the best in the Sci-Fi Channel seasons, and a genuine classic.

“You asked for an avalanche of flavor, and now you got it, huh? Not enjoying it, are you?”

While MST3K has always been known for its high volume of jokes, the Netflix seasons have a particular rushed delivery that can work against them. There are still a few great episodes in the two-season run, however, and Avalanche is a dark horse contender for the best of the lot.

Avalanche is a 1978 disaster movie produced by schlock auteur Roger Corman, starring Rock Hudson and Mia Farrow, who have less than zero chemistry with one another. They play a divorced couple, and it's obvious within seconds of seeing them together that there were multiple good reasons for that divorce.

That isn't Avalanche's biggest problem, however. In the best low-budget tradition, it saves all its special effects for the finale, which makes it a disaster movie where the titular disaster doesn't show up until the last 20 minutes. That leaves the viewer to sit through an hour of awkward foreshadowing, personal dramas, and horrible '70s dinner parties (there's a baked Alaska in Avalanche that's so unappetizing that it deserves its own unique content warning) until half the cast gets murdered by snow. The MST3K crew makes the best of it with some of the best jokes in season 11. It's an unsung hero of Jonah Ray's time as MST3K's host.

#3425. One Of Star Trek's Best Spock Episodes Is Hidden In The Series You Never Watched

One of the best Spock-forward episodes of the "Star Trek" franchise, "Yesteryear," is hidden deep in "Star Trek: The Animated Series." The show ran for two seasons from 1973 to 1974, and it is, in some ways, superior to "Star Trek: The Original Series." At the very least, because it's a 30-minute program, it's the more efficient show, having to tell similarly expansive sci-fi stories in half the time of "The Original Series."

Case in point: "Yesteryear" sees Kirk (William Shatner) and Spock (Leonard Nimoy) conducting time travel experiments with the Guardian of Forever, a living, stone-like time portal previously seen in the franchise-changing "Original Series" episode "The City on the Edge of Forever." After a sojourn to the past, though, something seems to have gone wrong with causality, and history has altered. No one can remember Spock, and an Andorian man has replaced him as the first officer of the USS Enterprise. This is a new, unfamiliar timeline.

Kirk and Spock look up the historical records in this new timeline and find that its version of Spock died at age seven back on Vulcan, poisoned by a catlike beast called a le-matya. Spock recalls, however, being saved from the le-matya by a cousin named Selek. Upon reflection, Kirk realizes that this mysterious Selek was likely Spock, having come from the future. The pair logically deduce that Spock needs to go back in time, pose as Selek, and save his seven-year-old self from a monster.

But the drama of "Yesteryear" delves deeper than a mere rescue mission. Indeed, the episode transforms into a thoughtful character piece about the decisions we make as children and the people we become as a result.

Spock, as you might recall, is half-human, and "Yesteryear" reveals that this was once a source of consternation for him. In fact, Spock was mocked and bullied as a child for his human blood, and he struggled between identifying as either human or Vulcan. He was once teetering on an important life question: will he choose the path of passionate human emotion or analytical Vulcan logic?

At age seven, the young Spock (Billy Simpson) is poised to undergo a coming-of-age ritual called the kahs-wan, a ritual that will prove his Vulcan-hood, yet he's initially unsure if he is prepared. The adult Spock gets to be present for this, and while the character is not emotional, viewers will likely wince when they see young Spock being bullied. Adult Spock has already chosen the path of logic, of course, but we can imagine his inner pain. How would you react to witnessing your own childhood bullying? Recall that adult Spock, while facing this, is also on a mission to repair time and needs to ensure that his childhood self chooses a Vulcan path. For a spell, then, he gets to be his own adult guardian.

The tension of "Yesteryear" involves young Spock trekking into the desert to undergo the kahs-wan ritual a month ahead of time. He has something to prove, you see, and takes his beloved childhood pet, a bear-dog named I-Chaya, as he prepares to spend a prolonged period surviving in the desert wilderness. And while the young Spock struggles to defend himself from the local fauna, adult Spock is, luckily, nearby to protect him from a le-matya attack. Unfortunately, this leads to a very difficult decision for young Spock.

During the scuffle, I-Chaya, is injured by the le-matya. A healer is then brought in and informs young Spock that although he can heal I-Chaya, it would lead to a long life full of struggle and intense pain for them. The young Spock, although caring deeply for his pet, logically deduces that euthanizing him is the logical, merciful decision.

It's this decision that leads Spock toward a life of logic. He chooses the path of being a Vulcan. It's a hard-won decision, yet it allows Spock to become who he's meant to be.

"Yesteryear" was penned by D.C. Fontana, who was involved with the "Star Trek" franchise on through to the early days of "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" in the early 1990s. Fontana even went on record about how she corrected some issues with the "Next Generation" series bible, and she is best known to Trekkies for having written classic "Original Series" episodes like "This Side of Paradise," "Journey to Babel," and "The Enterprise Incident." She also served as a story editor on "The Animated Series" and definitely had an ear for excellent sci-fi stories (having additionally contributed to the underrated Marvel animated series "Silver Surfer," and written episodes of shows like "Earth: Final Conflict" and "ReBoot").

"Yesteryear" explores Spock's past better than any "Star Trek" episode before it, and it should be pored over by Trekkies everywhere. That it's part of the woefully under-seen "Animated Series" means that it remains largely obscure to mainstream audiences. But it needn't be, as it's readily available to watch on Paramount+. For that matter, you should watch all of "The Animate Series." Think of it as the final two years of the five-year mission from "The Original Series."
