#3424. The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’

Rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works. Related Stories ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’

The scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”

For Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”

According to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as New York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn said. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”

Bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”

“She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”

For Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic said. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

“When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic said. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”

Coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn said, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”

The greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn said. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was important to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is currently streaming on the PBS app and website.

#3423. Why Rachel McAdams Turned Down The Role Of Pepper Potts In Marvel's Iron Man

As Tony Stark's (Robert Downey Jr.) girl Friday and eventual wife Pepper Potts, Gwyneth Paltrow is one of the longest lasting Marvel Cinematic Universe actors. She portrayed Pepper throughout the very first MCU film, 2008's "Iron Man," and was last seen in 2019's "Avengers: Endgame." Then again, it's also a meme that Paltrow barely remembers details of the Marvel movies she was in, down to forgetting altogether how she appeared in "Spider-Man: Homecoming."

Paltrow was not the "Iron Man" team's original first choice for Pepper. In December 2006, Umberto Gonzalez of Latino Review reported that Marvel Studios sent the "Iron Man" script exclusively to Rachel McAdams, hoping to cast her as Pepper. McAdams was riding a rising tide, having broken out in 2004 by playing Regina George in "Mean Girls" and Allie Hamilton in "The Notebook." The following year, she also starred in Wes Craven's hit airplane thriller "Red Eye." It makes sense that Marvel would've want to hire her, especially with "Iron Man" not being a guaranteed hit back then, but she declined. That, of course, opened the door for Paltrow's casting.

Speaking to Bustle in 2023, McAdams noted "Iron Man" was just one of several blockbusters she turned down in that time period, including "Casino Royale," "Mission: Impossible III," and "The Devil Wears Prada." Why? Simple, she'd been swept up off her feet into movie stardom and wanted to readjust with time for herself. Looking at McAdams' filmography, you'll notice she was largely on an acting break between 2006 and 2008 — she appeared in only two films (2007's "Married Life" and 2008's "The Lucky Ones") in that stretch.

"I knew I was in such a lucky spot, but I also knew it wasn't quite jiving with my personality and what I needed to stay sane," McAdams told Bustle.

Rachel McAdams' decision to take a break hardly killed her Hollywood momentum. To this day, McAdams enjoys a very healthy acting career, with her accolades including a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for "Spotlight." Amusingly, the first blockbuster she accepted a part in after her semi-hiatus was the 2009 "Sherlock Holmes" movie, directed by Guy Ritchie and starring... Robert Downey Jr., who'd just had his leading man status bolstered higher than ever by "Iron Man."

McAdams stars in "Sherlock Holmes" as the thief Irene Adler, Holmes' love interest. Now, Irene is more Catwoman (arguably the original Catwoman) than Pepper Potts, but "Sherlock Holmes" still shows McAdams and RDJ had chemistry aplenty. It's the closest we can get to tangible proof that, had she played Pepper, "Iron Man" (and the Marvel movies that followed) would've turned out just fine.

Marvel Studios didn't forget McAdams' number, either, considering she eventually starred in "Doctor Strange" as Dr. Christine Palmer, Stephen Strange's (Benedict Cumberbatch) ex. (Literally casting the woman who turned down Pepper Potts definitely makes "Doctor Strange" feel even more like wizard "Iron Man" than it already does.) McAdams later returned for the sequel, "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," which introduced her to director Sam Raimi.

Raimi, believing "Doctor Strange" wasn't the best showcase for McAdams, promised himself to work with her again. He thus cast McAdams in his subsequent movie, the survival thriller comedy "Send Help," featuring McAdams as an overlooked office drone who gets stuck on a desert island with her a-hole boss (Dylan O'Brien). "Send Help" features McAdams' most delightfully twisted performance yet — but if she'd agreed to "Iron Man" all those years ago, it's quite possible the dominos of her career would've fallen differently.

#3422. Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work

The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they showed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance. Related Stories The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’ ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner

“It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

“In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she said. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so important. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”

#3421. No Sci-Fi Series Does Dystopian Worldbuilding Better Than Netflix's 34-Episode Masterpiece

Worldbuilding is a vital component of any sci-fi series, but especially when it comes to the dystopian subgenre. These shows can't just rely on a tyrannical villain or hideous monster to chill viewers; the story's reality needs to be terrifying by itself. George Orwell's 1984 isn't the touchstone of dystopian storytelling because Big Brother is a great antagonist, but because the alternate future Orwell describes is vividly and unapologetically unsettling.

The elites of dystopian TV operate on a similar premise. The Handmaid's Tale crafts a devastatingly miserable political landscape, while 12 Monkeys blends dystopian tropes with mind-bending sci-fi to glorious effect. There isn't exactly a shortage of great dystopian TV shows out there, but there is one standing head and shoulders above the rest.

Running for seven seasons (and a film!) across both Channel 4 and Netflix, Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror has pierced pop culture like a spear through Brie. The phrase "like Black Mirror" has taken on a life of its own as a way to describe social and technological developments that give us the heebie-jeebies. That never would have happened unless Black Mirror had a knack for creating dystopian futures that haunt us, but the show's worldbuilding prowess is even more impressive than you realize.

The vast majority of sci-fi shows, especially those dwelling within the dystopian realm, are serialized in nature, meaning they enjoy the advantage of building fictional worlds across multiple episodes or seasons. In theory, more time means more detail, and more detail means a more fully-formed dystopia develops.

It's a credit to Charlie Brooker that Black Mirror achieves a more powerful effect despite telling separate stories in every episode. Each installment has only an hour or so to convey its dystopian setting, often using only a handful of characters and locations, and yet Black Mirror's vision of the future is almost always more emotionally affecting than a multi-season rivals with one story running all the way through.

Black Mirror boasts an uncanny ability to weave large dystopian worlds using smaller, more personal narratives. "Metalhead" never explains why civilization has collapsed or where the robot dogs came from, but Bella perfectly captures the desperation of humanity's survivors. Maxine Peake's performance gets across the hope, the fear, and the ruthlessness of the episode's dystopia better than most shows manage within an entire season, and it's those emotions that embed themselves deep into viewers' minds.

"Plaything" takes the opposite approach, chronicling the very moment human society falls into the post-apocalyptic hands of a sentient computer program, acting as an origin story for a dystopia we never truly get to see. Once again, however, the story orbits entirely around the emotional impact of these events upon one man: Peter Capaldi's Cameron.

Black Mirror's worldbuilding is head and shoulders above other sci-fi shows because instead of asking 'how did the world end?' it asks 'how was the life of this one specific individual destroyed?' For viewers, that personal touch offers the more harrowing experience, even when compared against long-running shows that contextualize their dystopias in painstaking detail. It's telling that, going back to 1984, Orwell's book essentially does the same thing with Winston. It's the POV character study that makes 1984 so unnerving.

Black Mirror also honors the longstanding horror rule that what you don't see is scarier than what you do, and each of its dystopian episodes carry a sense of unseen mystery. Indeed, it's the same unseen mystery every time: the vague suggestion that different parts of Black Mirror are secretly connected.

"Plaything" being a sequel to "Bandersnatch" creates a sense of impending doom. And the notion that the post-apocalypse from "Metalhead" can be traced back to Michael Callow's ham sandwich in "The National Anthem" creates a grim sense of inevitable destruction across the entire series. It's almost like a deeper, darker conspiracy is bubbling beneath the show's surface. It's a nagging, worrying sensation that only makes Black Mirror's dystopian universe even harder to shake out of our heads when an episode's end credits roll.

#3420. 10 Action Video Games That Are Bangers From Start to Finish

When it comes to video games, some of the most popular have always been the likes of action/adventure titles. Video games provide a great escape for the player. Giving them the chance to be an action hero, swinging around New York City, stealing cars, shooting up bad guys, or becoming the samurai of their dreams makes them as popular as they've become.

Like any genre of any medium, though, there are some games that most certainly stand out among the others. This isn't to say that they're better than all the rest—there are too many games to make such an objective statement—but there are some certified bangers that come to mind when the discussion of action video games begins.

This wonderful series by Rocksteady Studios is known as one of the best superhero video game franchises of all time, and for very good reason. A lot of those reasons were either expanded upon from the first game, or established in the second title, Batman: Arkham City. This is known as one of the best superhero games out there, and has gone down in history for it.

Batman: Arkham City is well-known for the common notion that it makes you truly feel like Batman (Kevin Conroy). The gameplay mechanics are very well-executed, and the story is thrilling from start to finish. Not to mention, the return of Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as Joker is a huge win and makes this truly feel like some of the many definitive versions of the characters.

If there's one thing PlayStation is excellent at, it's having some amazing console-exclusive titles. One of the best of recent years is none other than Horizon Zero Dawn. Following the hunter known as Aloy (Ashly Burch), Horizon Zero Dawn takes players on a journey of trying to discover the truth about the hunter's origins, and, in turn, the world around her itself.

This project takes place in a post-apocalyptic setting, but not in the manner of another PlayStation exclusive, The Last of Us. The landscape of Horizon Zero Dawn is wide, vast, and filled with high-technology—machine creatures that are now the apex predators, to be exact. The combat—using Aloy's hunting skills and weapons—is wonderful, and such a blast to play. Not to mention, this new world is such a joy to explore and keeps the players actively wanting to discover more about it via the story and the open-world nature of the title.

When it comes to action, there are few that bring the amount that Hades does. That's because the entire point of the game is, well, action. While there is a story to Hades, the game, at its heart, is a rougelike dungeon crawler title that puts the player against hoards and rooms upon rooms of foes to face as the son of Hades (Logan Cunningham), Zagreus (Darren Korb), attempts to escape the Underworld.

Players will die but, every time they begin anew, they can spend their hard-earned resources to level up and go at it again with new powers. The method to the madness of Hades is failing, trying again, failing, and going until the player finally makes it through. It is an absolute thrill ride the entire way through.

While Sega is most known for the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, they have another video game series that is widely beloved, Yakuza. The best game in said series is none other than Yazuka 0. The Yakuza series is a great time, and the way it brings together gritty crime drama with some hilarious comedy that keeps the players on their toes.

As stated, the best of the best, Yakuza 0, brings all of these things to the table and enhances them. It follows two stories simultaneously, and that really helps in keeping the players invested. The combat mechanics are phenomenal and the true, main highlight of the game. Yakuza 0 is truly the perfect example of how to make an incredible Yazkua game.

While the recent God of War games are easily some of the best PlayStation titles in recent years, if fans of action want something in the series to seriously deliver on that, they need to look no further than God of War II. This sequel truly delivers on action, spectacle, and fun gameplay. It has a blockbuster-level story that is engaging for the entire runtime.

Not to forget, the players get to take on the gods of Olympus. Kratos (Terrence "T.C." Carson) is out for blood, and he is going to stop at nothing to get it. This allows players to experience some serious spectacle as they fight their way through Olympus and take down the gods. It's a ride filled with intensity till the very end and worth playing every second.

Much like Batman: Arkham City, Insomniac Games' hit title, Marvel's Spider-Man, is well-regarded because of how much it makes the player truly feel like Spider-Man (Yuri Lowenthal). The swinging physics/mechanics are stellar, and easily some of the best in any Spider-Man game ever. Swinging mechanics are so much more important to a Spider-Man game than one would realize on paper. For quite some time, Spider-Man 2's video game was known to have the best.

Many consider it one of the best modern superhero video games of all time. The execution of Marvel's Spider-Man was done with grace and prowess. This reimagining of the Spider-Man world—where Peter Parker is older, experienced, and facing off with enemies he's never faced before—is so well-done, and it's a fan-favorite Spider-Man universe. Playing Marvel's Spider-Man truly does make the player feel like Spider-Man, and, alongside that, has an astounding story.

There are a few things in this life that will always be cool: cowboys, superheroes, spacemen, and . . . samurais. A modern game that might genuinely capture the samurai vibe the best is none other than 2020's Ghost of Tsushima. If there's one thing that can describe this game, it's that it is vastly cinematic. It feels like players are playing through a classic samurai film.

Playing the ever-gorgeous Ghost of Tsushima feels like playing through a movie in all the best ways. The camera, shot framing, battles, and more all make this story amazing to experience. The melee combat is borderline perfect. Sword duels and other action feel so natural and exhilarating to play—it's genuinely difficult to put this amazing game down.

2016's Doom is about as action-packed as it gets. It is a literal non-stop space adventure that has players firing bullets of all kinds into horrifying monsters. Doom rewards players for being aggressive and jumping straight into action, rather than strategy. There is always a battle or chase going down, and it never stops being abundantly exciting.

But players aren't just firing the same kind of gun the entire time—no, there is a gigantic arsenal of weapons players will have the choice to utilize throughout the entire game. Just as importantly, the score behind the action is one of the best action game scores of all time. Composed by the legendary Mick Gordon, everything that is great about Doom is enhanced by Gordon's excellent work.

Another sword-wielding adventure—reminiscent of Ghost of Tsushima—from recent years that is phenomenal is the ever-thrilling Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Taking place in the late-1500s, this 2019 adventure follows a shinobi named Sekiro (Daisuke Namikawa and Noshir Dalal), players get to step into the shoes of an incredible swordsman as he goes on a journey to rescue his captured lord, Kuro (Miyuki Sato and Amber Hood).

Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is everything a typical FromSoftware game—Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Elden Ring—is, in all the best ways. It truly challenges the player in ways other FromSoftware titles don't. It also has a setting unlike the others, too, being set in 1500s Japan. It is so distinct, vast, and exciting that it feels like a must-play for those who love some good sword combat . . . even if it has the classic tough FromSoftware difficuly.

There is absolutely no question that Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest game of the decade—maybe even the last two decades. People have been waiting for this game for so long that the cultural impact has been increasing little by little every year, exploding in one great release this year. Ask anyone who's played it, and they'll most likely say, "It was worth the wait."

This game is truly something special. It has attention to detail unlike any other, gorgeous visuals, skilled performances, groundbreaking mechanics across the board, and a wonderful story at the core of it all. There are dozens of reasons to love this game, but one of the main highlights are the action sequences—of which there are plenty. Robberies, assassinations, gunfights, etc. bring Grand Theft Auto VI to the top of the "best of all time" list.

#3417. Final Fantasy 9 Sequel Officially Releasing 2028

The Final Fantasy series has enjoyed a lot more ups than downs over the years, but most fans agree that the ninth mainline game in the series is one of the very best. The game's greatest strength is undoubtedly its narrative, and the cast of characters who bring it life, many of whom still serve as the most memorable protagonists we have seen to date.

Add to that a return to the medieval fantasy roots that had made the series so popular in the first place, and Square Enix were never going to be on to anything other than a big winner. Though the developer doesn't traditionally do direct sequels in their mainline games in the series, it sure would have been nice to pick up the story of this one elsewhere, even in a spin-off.

Happily, that's all about to change, but it isn't in a medium that you might expect.

As first reported by GameDaily, Final Fantasy IX: The Black Mages' Legacy is an upcoming animated series that's back in development, after spending plenty of time in limbo. The project was first announced back in 2021 by Cyber Group Studios, a Paris-based animation company, after they secured the rights to partner with Square Enix.

They then spent the best part of three years trying to sell the product to licensees, seemingly without much in the way of success, before they entered financial difficulties in October 2024. After that, four potential buyers expressed their interest in securing the rights to the assets and IPs of the comapny, before EuroVisual came out with approximately 80% of them, including Final Fantasy, in March 2025.

Now, the 2D animated series has appeared on the company's official website as officially in development, with a first season of ten 22-minute episodes and a tentative targeted release date of 2028. The series is being aimed at children between the ages of 8 and 13, with supervision from Square Enix designed to ensure the story remains consistent with the game.

So what narrative will the story follow? The series is set to pick up around ten years after the original game, with the children of Vivi Ornitier, six young black mages named Mel, Koln, Luciola, Théa, Fala, and Doc, who are living in the city of Alexandria.

Anybody who has played the game will know the emotional weight that Vivi's character arc has, and the series is likely to touch on similar themes, only through the prism of his offspring. We don't have specific details beyond that just yet, but it could absolutely be one to watch for old fans, despite its usual target audience.

Outside of that, Final Fantasy fans also have the concluding part of the Remake trilogy of the seventh game to look forward to. Titled Revelation, it's set to drop on April 7, 2027 for PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S, and PC, finally bringing to a close the retelling of one of the best games of all time in the process.

Especially compared to the likes of literature, theater, and film, whose histories go back over 100 years of history, video games are a much newer artform of creative expression that is still taking shape and evolving year by year. Still, the medium has had an undeniable growth since the early days of arcade shooters and 8-bit graphics, as games are able to tell rich and powerful stories all while being more immersive than any other artform. Especially with Grand Theft Auto VI's recent record-breaking release further cementing video games as the dominant entertainment medium of the modern age, it places an even greater legacy on the games designated as the greatest of all time.

What makes for a truly exceptional video game experience is going to vary and differ from each individual person, as there is no truly 100% correct list of the greatest video games of all time. For the sake of this list, the entries are a collection of games that consistently stand out and come up in conversation not just because of their high quality, but because of the standards they set when they released and their influence on the entire medium. Still, this only scratches the surface of exceptional video games that have been released since the inception of the industry.

While many people may think of the long-running television franchise or even the original comic when it comes to The Walking Dead, gamers will immediately sing the praises of Telltale's legendary point-and-click adventure game. An original story set in the comic book universe, the episodic game set a new standard for emotional storytelling and writing in video games, with a rich narrative influenced by player choice that amplifies the greatest strengths of Robert Kirkman's original series.

With stylish cell-shaded graphics and approachable gameplay simple enough for even casual gamers to enjoy and get wrapped up in the story, Telltale's The Walking Dead does a great job of making its central story as engaging and impactful as possible. While Telltale has continued the story with an array of subsequent sequels and continuing story, it's the original run of 5 episodes that made such a massive impact on audiences as one of the most poignant and beautiful gaming experiences of all time.

In the early days of 8-bit video games, the platformer genre reigned supreme as the most widely popular style of gaming, with no platformer franchise being as popular or immediately recognizable as Super Mario Bros. While the original NES classic is exceptional enough as it is, the brilliance and timeless appeal of the Mario franchise wouldn't be fully realized until Super Mario Bros. 3, which almost 40 years later is still one of the best 2d platformers ever made.

The game absolutely perfects the feeling and smooth controls required of a platformer of the era, being leaps and bounds ahead of its contemporaries in terms of precision and game feel. This is all on top of the overwhelming creativity in terms of the game's level designs and power-ups that truly bring the wild chaos of the Mario world to life. This classic platformer still stands as the absolute best game released on the Nintendo Entertainment System.

A striking monolith of the action-adventure genre from Team Ico, PlayStation 2 classic Shadow of the Colossus has stood as one of the quintessential examples of games as serious art ever since its release. The game features staggering visuals and a gargantuan sense of scale, seeing the player have to face off against various massive creatures across the land with the goal of resurrecting a young woman. Through traversing the world on horse and by foot, its exceptional visuals and minimalist design come together to create a defining gaming experience.

Especially in an era where action adventure gaming was continuously getting louder and more abrasive with its gameplay and visuals, the slow and methodical approach that Shadow of the Colossus took made the game that much more striking and memorable to 2000s gamers. It truly felt ahead of its time in terms of being an interactive work of art, with something meaningful and sorrowful to say in its storytelling instead of pure entertainment.

One of the premiere masterpieces of the PlayStation brand and one of the first games that come to mind for many when considering games that actively go for a cinematic feel, The Last of Us is one of the defining gaming masterpieces of the 2010s. It tells a dark post-apocalyptic story that primarily focuses on the loss of humanity at large, paralleling the unlikely connection that fosters between a smuggler who lost his daughter and a young girl who has only known this apocalyptic world.

While the emotional and groundbreaking storytelling is the primary element that people praise about The Last of Us, the core stealth-centric action gameplay is also worthy of praise, as it gets the player engaged and immersed in this heightened world where anything can go wrong. The game was also for many a massive leap forward in terms of technical craft in visuals, pushing the PlayStation 3 to its limits and ushering in a new age of realism in video games.

One of the great advents of gaming as an artform becoming more accessible in the digital era is that many more independent game developers are able to bring their visions to life, with a wide array of indie game masterpieces being released in the 21st century. One of the most defining and culturally dominant indie games has been Undertale, Toby Fox's quaint and quirky mixture of RPGs like Earthbound and bullet hell games like Touhou Project.

More than anything else, Undertale thrives thanks to its overwhelming charm and ingenuity, utilizing simplistic visuals and dynamic gameplay to create an experience that consistently delights and surprises the player. It certainly has a goofy tongue-in-cheek tone, satirizing many tropes of RPGs and video games as a whole, but there are also a lot of immaculate character writing and exceptional secrets that make Undertale one of the most influential indie games of all time.

An icon of the metroidvania genre so influential that the very genre is in part coined after its exceptional non-linear design, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night is the undeniable high point of a franchise that has delivered gaming greatness ever since the early days of 8-bit consoles. The game originally sold poorly due to being a 2D game released on a console that famously was at the forefront of early 3D gaming, the original PlayStation, but word of mouth about its quality transformed Symphony of the Night into one of gaming's greatest sleeper hits.

The game famously utilized a non-linear approach to the classic concept of exploring Dracula's Castle, allowing the player all sorts of freedom in the order in which they explore the castle and progress through the story. Combined with an incredibly addictive gameplay loop that has the player actively feel their character grow and get stronger as they play, Symphony of the Night has been the standard for non-linear metroidvanias for nearly 3 decades.

The Legend of Zelda series has continuously released some of the most important and widely influential adventures ever made, dating back 40 years of groundbreaking video game experiences. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild is the best-selling game in the series, as it completely reinvented and redefined what a Zelda game could be in the modern age and becoming one of the all-time greatest open world games.

Breath of the Wild was a game defined by its sense of pure freedom as an open world adventure, giving the player more control in terms of the order that they go about events compared to any other adventure game at the time, even able to go right to the final boss from the very beginning. Combined with a dynamic physics system and an overwhelming amount of charm and attention to detail, Breath of the Wild has been the quintessential Nintendo masterpiece of the past 10 years.

A story-based RPG that utilizes tabletop mechanics as the centric for its gameplay and setting, Disco Elysium is a masterclass of narrative and storytelling in the medium of video games. It's very abstract as far as RPGs are concerned, having very little combat and instead utilizing its RPG mechanics as skill checks for various actions and dialogue trees, much like a tabletop game would. This classic gameplay loop makes for one of the most immersive and limitless stories in gaming history, branching out into a wide array of different possibilities entirely dependent on player choice.

Its prospects as an indie game allow Disco Elysium not to hold back in terms of the symbolic themes and messaging of its story, commending on so many different aspects of life, government, and ideology in a game rich with perfectly written dialogue across the board. Disco Elysium is one of the greatest works of art that modern gaming has to offer, and is an absolute must-play for anyone who appreciates a great story in video games.

Once video games started to get larger in scale and complexity, the turn-based RPG inspired by games like Dungeons & Dragons became one of the best showcases for an immersive, long-lasting adventure; with Square being one of the best studios for RPGs in the classic era. One of several iconic Square RPGs was Chrono Trigger, a time traveling adventure sporting character designs from Dragon Ball creator Akira Toriyama that quickly became heralded as an RPG masterpiece.

The game has an immediately engaging story, following a group of adventurers from across time who work together to prevent a global catastrophe. While many other RPGs of the 20th century would largely focus on classic fantasy archetypes and elements, Chrono Trigger acted as this sprawling mixture of fantasy and sci-fi elements that was incredibly unique for the time. Mixed with immaculate storytelling and a perfect original soundtrack, to create one of the first times that a game fully enthralled and enchanted players as a complete experience.

Outer Wilds is one of the greatest examples of how, even in the modern age of video games, there are exciting and groundbreaking original concepts still being made that completely reshape and redefine what a video game can be. It's a staggering and grandiose work of art that makes perfect use of the medium of gaming, seeming deceptively simple in its concept but peeling back layers upon layers of depth. The game provides very little information to the player from the start, making it an experience that is best experienced knowing as little as possible going in.

What can be mentioned is the game's base premise, as it sees the player exploring a planetary system that is stuck in a 22-minute time loop that ends in the entire system being destroyed when its sun goes supernova. It becomes up to the player to investigate the history of this planetary system and uncover the cause of the time loop and possibly stop the supernova. Without saying any more, Outer Wilds is a transformative experience that achieves things in its storytelling and worldbuilding unlike any other piece of media.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3415. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3414. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

With my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique new design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

If they make one the size of the iPhone 13 mini I will buy. Otherwise I'm holding out

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

What do you think of the rumored iPhone 20 Pro design? Let us know in the comments.

#3413. Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’

[Editor’s note: The following interview contains spoilers for “La Bola Negra.”]

With a head of hair, lithe frame, and the soft eyes Caravaggio would’ve loved if the Italian painter were Spanish, pop star Guitarricadelafuente is having a monumental year on- and off-screen. The gay 29-year-old songwriter finished touring his sensational, sensually charged second album “Spanish Leather” earlier this fall, and only just a few short months after his screen debut, “La Bola Negra,” won a Cannes top prize, got scooped up by Netflix, and entered the awards season fray.

Oscar talk is in the wind, not just for his performance as queer closeted trumpeter Sebastián, who joins the Nationalist forces during the Spanish Civil War to survive, but for writing the original song “La Nieve.” The sweeping ballad ties together the film’s three story threads that convene around queer Spanish playwright Federico García Lorca’s incomplete text: 1932, 1937 (Sebastián’s storyline), and 2017. Born Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, he’s now a meme thanks to his stage and screen sobriquet, which means “little guitar of the fountain.” Related Stories ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier John Turturro, Carrie Coon, Guitarricadelafuente, and Peter Gamble to Receive SFFILM Honors

Guitarricadelafuente’s performance balances both hushed repression and eventually unleashed emotions throughout “La Bola Negra,” as Sebastián nurses wounded (and handsome) Republican soldier Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau, a more established actor in Spain). They fall for each other in the process, in a furtive romance mostly framed in stolen glances and tacit looks — in other words, the sort of good old-fashioned gay yearning that’s made movies like “Brokeback Mountain,” “Call Me by Your Name,” and “God’s Own Country” so popular. “La Bola Negra” is, by now, one of the highest-grossing Spanish movies ever to play in Spain, and it’s a major Oscar contender in select theaters as it gears up for its early December Netflix streaming premiere.

IndieWire spoke to Guitarricadelafuente over Zoom where, behind him, an oversized window frame flanked the waves gently rushing up to Miami Beach. Below, we discuss his songwriting process for “La Nieve,” witnessing the breakup of directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo (which happened during filming), and how he overcame his fears to make his auspicious screen debut. That’s all while balancing a proudly out music career where his sexuality is front and center. Plus, watch an exclusive video about his role in the film at the bottom of this story.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You’ve been all over the world with “La Bola Negra,” from Cannes in May to Toronto and, now, Miami Beach for this virtual junket interview. You’re used to being all over the place. You also toured your album this year. Did that help you prepare for promoting the film?

Guitarricadelafuente: I would say that kind of, in a way, because there’s something that I see as very similar to going and talking about the movie and talking about your character, which is something very similar to when you’re going around touring with your album. I think it’s more difficult because you need to talk about yourself and not just about playing a character because the music you make comes from a very profound place, and you need to talk about many things that go inside of you.

This is your acting debut, and there’s Oscar chatter for both your performance and the song you wrote for the film, “La Nieve.” Do you watch the Academy Awards in Spain?

Not that much recently, but I remember when I was studying architecture in college, I used to stay up late at night doing projects. I remember staying up until 3:00 a.m. and with my friends, we were doing our little houses, and we would put the television on, and see the awards. But that was one of the only times that I stayed up late, or that I used to stay up late to see the awards, because you always receive that in Spain in the morning after.

You signed up for the movie without a script. What was the pitch that the Javis gave you? You knew you’d have to learn the trumpet.

They didn’t tell me that I had to learn an instrument because it was going to be originally something that I already knew how to play, but they wanted to make it more difficult. So they said, “OK, why don’t you try a trumpet?” But yeah, the first pitch, there was not much about it. They told me about “La piedra oscura” by Alberto Conejero, which was the original play where the characters of Rafael and Sebastián appear.

I just knew that it was going to be set against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, with Lorca being so present. … They didn’t convince me, but I was so moved by how they were so confident that I could do it because I was so frightened and I wasn’t sure at all, but it was their vision. I admired them so much from before. I knew that they’ve worked with many nonprofessional actors, and people acting for the first time. So it was something that I just threw myself into.

You were frightened about whether or not you could deliver as an actor, or was it the material?

I was spending all of my time making music and touring, and it was very time-consuming and exhausting. … I didn’t know if I could put myself into that experience because I thought the proper way to dig into that role was to put your soul into it.

They were looking for someone who was openly gay for this role, right? There’s a spectrum of sexualities among the cast. Miguel Bernardeau, your scene partner, is straight.

Well, I don’t even know if we talked about that at any point because it was just assumed that I was. [Laughs] I don’t know if that was a condition. I think it was something that, to be more faithful to the story, had to happen. At the time that they approached me with the role, I was finishing my last album, “Spanish Leather.” It represented an imaginary — but not that imaginary — journey of a young gay man who comes out from his village and puts himself out to the world, discovering who he is and where he belongs.

Many people would know my music, but I would realize that not many people knew that I was gay even. There’s a big, not sexual, but I would say sensual component to [“Spanish Letter”] and this process of growing up and sexual [awakening]. So it was very special in a way to play this role … it’s something that you don’t get that much, maybe in Spain, just to see things where you can get referenced with or reflected with.

Los Javis broke up during production. Did they communicate that to the cast? How did you find out?

It was so weird because I don’t know if I’m stupid or what, I didn’t even notice. I would hear obviously so many rumors, but … you couldn’t tell that they were apart because they were acting as one. And I couldn’t believe that they were breaking up with the intensity of that shoot. It was like, “How on earth are they going to split up in the middle of this craziness and this madness?”

But I don’t even remember when they told us. I think it was at the end of the shoot. We would eventually know that something was going on. I couldn’t believe it. How have you managed to carry this shoot? But that also represented how moving this story was to them.

Of course. Even when they reached out to me with the role, I would hear rumors, and I was like, “How is this going to be possible if they’re so tight together?” It was inevitable because they are so well known in Spain, that rumors would arrive.

Miguel has probably 10 years of acting experience that you don’t have. Was he helpful as a mentor, as well as an onscreen romance?

The first time that we met, it was actually when he was doing his audition because the only character that was clear in the movie was Sebastián. We had to test how this approach was going to be with the real Rafael, because this very tight and intimate connection had to happen. He didn’t know that I was going to play Sebastián, and he just appeared in the rehearsal room. And I thought there was a very special instant connection there, that I think we’re obviously very different, or we come from very different backgrounds or different ways of seeing the world.

But there was a beauty in that because obviously I saw him as this wonderful, beautiful, talented, and professional actor that I could anchor myself in. He’s all the time lying on a bed [on screen]. And so he has to say so many things without being able to move. We were both left a lot of freedom on set and to try and to make errors. The room would get empty, and it was just Los Javis, Miguel, and I.

Were you writing the movie’s theme song, “La Nieve,” during production?

It was a very long process from the beginning, when I was told to write the song. I don’t think of me doing a song as in I get into a room and say, “OK, what I’m going to talk about right now?” And then I get a lyric, and I go back home. This Film has so many stories in it, and to try to be faithful to all of them and try to unify them in a thread, in a song, was very difficult. I was listening at the time, before they reached out to me, to Spanish Civil War songs.

It was actually a queer singer of the time who was called Rolando Alarcón. There were songs played with parlor guitars that were [made] to be sung on the waterfront. We started preparing the role with Los Javis. Lorca had to be very present also in this because he’s all over the place. He’s pretty omnipresent all of the time, surveilling what’s going on. And you had to pay a homage to him because, in the end, “La bola negra” was this unfinished script that he was writing.

I had to live my character in my own skin and properly carry that emotional baggage that he was holding. And it wasn’t until the end of the shoot, when we were in Cantabria living for two months … I obviously had this melody in my head, but when this scene with the firing squad happens, and [SPOILER ALERT] Rafael dies, it was a combination of all of that emotional journey that the character was living.

I would arrive home that day and start playing a melody on a piano and mumbling some lyrics, and I would send this to Los Javis, and I didn’t know that they were going to use this to unify the three stories that go on in the movie. And it was a way for me to let all of that emotion go.

This song will now have to be part of every setlist you perform. It’s your “My Heart Will Go On.”

I hope it turns into that. I wish to be 50 years old and be in Madrid and be singing that. That would be so beautiful. Because I feel that I was just playing in Madrid my last concert one month ago, it was kind of the closing chapter of this “Spanish Leather” tour, and the film was just released one week before that. And so I got the chance to play “La Nieve” there for the first time. After that, it was very emotional because you would hear 18,000 people singing to that. It was like goosebumps. After that, people would be commenting on TikTok, “So Sebastián had the chance to finally be a musician and get to Madrid and perform.” That’s kind of like a closing of the thread, a very beautiful thing.

“La Bola Negra” is also one of the highest-grossing Spanish movies to play in Spain ever. Have you been able to go home and experience that?

We were in Spain those first two weeks until we had the last concert in Madrid, and then we went to Toronto and all over the place. And that was a very special week because I was at my sister’s wedding. You could feel something in the air. There was a communal excitement, and people of all ages, all different ages, going to the cinema, or even people, like aunts of mine, who haven’t been to the cinema in 10 years, to see how that’s happening is something that makes us very proud.

For me, the Spanish premiere was more important because that’s all Spanish people’s lives. Everybody has been linked to that moment of time, it’s like their ancestors. So the Spanish were going to be the most critical of it. But to see how young people, old people, people from different backgrounds go and you suddenly have this sense of communion was something spectacular that you could see in the streets. Like older ladies and young queer guys coming up to you, it’s just incredible.

What are you doing next? Do you want to keep acting?

Yeah. It’s been a crazy time. I’m having the time to even make new music and to, I don’t know, to see what I’m able to, because even three years ago… I would oblige myself to be quiet and rest to be able to feel inspired. But now it’s all these hectic times that are making me feel so inspired, and to share that time and put it into making art.

“La Bola Negra” is now in select theaters will start streaming on Netflix on Wednesday, December 2.

#3411. 10-Part High Fantasy Series With Game Of Thrones Vibes Is Coming For GRRM's Crown

A 10-part high fantasy series with Games of Thrones vibes is coming for George R.R. Martin's crown, storming ahead on its own path. Game of Thrones is one of the best fantasy TV shows ever made, featuring a sweeping story that spans across Westeros with an ensemble cast of characters at the forefront. The series was a pioneer in breathtaking fantasy worlds coming to life on the small screen, at a time where such high-end production value was usually reserved for movie screens.

Since the series ended, there have been many fantasy TV shows that have tried to measure up, none of which have quite succeeded. While spinoffs like House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms have their own identities, nothing has matched the sweeping scope of the original. Netflix's The Witcher, Prime Video's The Wheel of Time, and the ongoing The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power have all tried to capture a similar approach and tone in their own fantasy stories, only managing a fraction of HBO's masterpiece.

But Apple TV might have cracked the code on how to make a TV show even bigger and better than the entire Game of Thrones franchise. In January 2026, Apple TV announced they had acquired the rights to books and stories in the Cosmere, interconnected fantasy stories penned by Brandon Sanderson. The author himself wrote a script for a Mistborn movie adaptation that Apple will be making for their streaming platform. But there's one other series that's getting a major TV treatment from the streamer.

That series is The Stormlight Archive, a high fantasy series following an ensemble cast of characters on the planet-sized supercontinent Roshar. The books follow its characters thousands of years after a massive war, as ancient and magical elements of the world once thought to have been lost forever begin to reemerge. So far, five books of the series have been published, serving as the first arc of the series. The second arc, also set to consist of five books, is expected to begin publication in 2031.

The Stormlight Archive is even more sweeping than Game of Thrones, with a major focus on war-torn battles, the mentality of its core characters, and a more high fantasy feel than HBO's series. While The Stormlight Archive isn't as graphic as Martin's book series, it does feature plenty of battles and major conflicts that will require a TV-MA rating to showcase. But its major characters, from the surgeon-turned-soldier Kaladin, to the noble spy Shallan, all have intriguing storylines that begin individually before, eventually, converging in spectacular fashion.

The Stormlight Archive doesn't just have a 10-book series to pull from to ensure the adaptation plays out properly. The books can also look at Game of Thrones' mistakes and learn lessons from them. For one, sticking to the books is a major key to success, considering going off-script is what led to the fantasy TV show's controversial final season. For another, The Stormlight Archive's books are all over 1,000 pages each, meaning it's important the show focuses on the most important elements, much like Game of Thrones did.

Since The Stormlight Archive is entering a world familiar with high fantasy TV series and concepts, it can learn a lot from its predecessor to be the best possible adaptation of Sanderson's series. Game of Thrones might have some steep competition if the series is done right, as the massive narrative of interconnected storylines means a very Westeros feel to the show. But, with a more classic fantasy adventure approach, it could be the best successor to Martin's work produced for a different franchise.

#3410. Disney Officially Decides the Fate of James Cameron’s ‘Avatar 4’

It's a fairly ridiculous position for James Cameron to find himself in when making almost $1.5 billion at the worldwide box office is considered something of a disappointment, but that's the problem with having directed three of the highest-grossing movies in the history of cinema. Having spent much of the last two decades on Pandora, Cameron has been increasingly vocal about his desire to make other movies, with his planned adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's The Devils and his long-gestating Hiroshima project among those he's particularly keen to get behind the camera for. Whether Cameron gets to make those movies before heading back to Pandora, however, has been one of the bigger questions surrounding Disney's upcoming theatrical slate.

Disney has officially included Avatar 4 in its upcoming theatrical release slate, with the movie featured during the studio's Upfronts presentation in Buenos Aires, Argentina, where the fourth movie was listed alongside the likes of Black Panther 3 and Incredibles 3, which is particularly encouraging given Cameron's own uncertainty about making another trip to Pandora after Avatar: Fire and Ash.

Of course, some of Avatar 4 has already been shot, and not just recently. Ages ago in fact, Cameron filmed scenes involving the younger members of the Sully family alongside the previous two movies, given that the fourth installment will feature a time jump of around six years. Trinity Jo-Li Bliss, who plays Tuk, was just nine years old when she filmed her earlier scenes for the fourth movie. She is now 17. Yes, that's how long ago.

Despite Avatar: Fire and Ash making around $1.48 billion worldwide, that's still considerably less than the $2.32 billion made by Avatar: The Way of Water, and Cameron has spoken about wanting to bring down both the cost of making the movies and the amount of time he spends making them. Executive producer Rae Sanchini, however, told Inverse earlier this year that preparations for the next two movies were already underway, with the team working on budgets, scheduling, and technology.

The cast of Fire and Ash includes Sam Worthington (Horizon: An American Saga) as Jake Sully, Zoe Saldaña (Guardians of the Galaxy) as Neytiri, Sigourney Weaver (Alien) as Kiri, Stephen Lang (Don't Breathe) as Miles Quaritch, Oona Chaplin (Game of Thrones) as Varang, Britain Dalton as Lo'ak, Jack Champion (Scream VI) as Spider, and Bliss as Tuk.

Avatar 4 remains scheduled for December 21, 2029, with Avatar 5 dated for December 19, 2031. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

#3408. Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination?

How will Robert Pattinson‘s casting as James Bond affect his Oscar chances? The hard-working star, who was established by the “Twilight” franchise, has ricocheted from Christopher Nolan projects (“Tenet” and “The Odyssey”) and the DC franchise’s “The Batman” (“Part Two” is shooting in London) to riskier indies like the Safdies’ “Good Time” and Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse.”

This award season, Pattinson was juggling three long-shot potential Oscar nods: Best Actor for A24’s marital deconstruction “The Drama,” and Supporting Actor for two Snidely Whiplash villains, lead suitor Antinous in Universal’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” and shape-shifter Scytale in Warner Bros.’ “Dune: Part Three,” respectively. His best chance at an Oscar nomination, though, was always for his creepy lead turn as TV journalist Chris Hansen in “Primetime,” another A24 release. Related Stories Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’ ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

When Daniel Craig was cast as James Bond during the awards tour for Steven Spielberg’s “Munich” (2005), the immediate result was a marked increase in attendance at all screenings, recalls one veteran publicist. “There was a different before-and-after energy,” he said. That did not land Craig a nomination, however. The only Bond to score an Oscar nod and win after a long and storied career was Sean Connery (“The Untouchables”). Playing Bond does not lend an actor cred with the Academy. But it does extend a career.

The impact for Pattinson, who is ubiquitous in online media, is the same. At this point, most awards voters will have seen “The Odyssey,” but those seeing the Christopher Nolan blockbuster for the first time will view the actor differently. “He will have heightened scrutiny,” said one studio Oscar expert. “Clearly he is being tapped to anchor a franchise. For the actors [branch], he will be someone to reckon with.”

Clearly, fewer people have screened “Primetime.” Pattinson’s Bond ascension will push the movie up in the must-see rankings. “Bond probably gets more people to watch the movie,” said one Oscar strategist. “That’s half the battle. The goal is to get people to watch the movie. But the movie has to do the work.”

At the box office, “Primetime” has fared better domestically ($47 million) than abroad ($12 million), which is significant given an Oscar voting pool of more than 10,000 voters, one-quarter of whom are international. How will “Primetime” do with the upcoming critic votes? Or BAFTAs, which will reveal the international tale? And SAG’s Actor Awards, where, at this stage, Gold Derby has “Digger” star Tom Cruise edging out Pattinson? The race between those two actors is “squishy,” said Debra Birnbaum, Gold Derby editor-in-chief, who distinguishes between early season “hopedictions” and “real predictions.”

It helps to remember that the Academy is just starting to catch up with the contenders. The experts on Gold Derby (I’m one), at this stage, have seen way more movies than the site’s users or the Academy. Later in the season, Gold Derby users and experts are more in sync. That’s why we should take with a grain of salt the recent ascension among the Gold Derby users to number five for Best Actor contender Pattinson. They’re responding to publicity. The experts have him at seven. The same is true for the betting site Kalshi’s odds. Their accuracy improves the closer you get to the Oscars. At this stage, their bettors haven’t seen everything. And the key Oscar season markers, from critics’ groups to Guild awards, haven’t played out.

The American Cinematheque came out way ahead by honoring Pattinson with its annual award fete, set to take place on February 9, 2027. Tables are selling out and Bond studio Amazon/MGM — and Hollywood — will be there in force.

While Pattinson has never been an actors’ actor, he’s a hugely bankable global movie star. He’s going to keep us interested for a long time.

#3406. Pokémon Gen 11 Sounds Like A Region-Spanning Dream Come True

There's no doubt that 2026 has been a really exciting year for Pokémon fans all over the world, as the franchise we have all grown up adoring finally celebrates its 30th birthday. That meant all kinds of exciting announcements from those continue to chart its course, and we got plenty of fascinating release designed to mark the occasion too.

Arguably the biggest of those was confirmation of the first games of the tenth generation, Winds and Waves, which are set to release in the latter half of 2027. The new region featured in those is based on the archipelagos of South-East Asia, and it looks like a major departure from anything else we've seen to date, something which the series has arguably needed after treading water for a while.

With that in mind, the fact that we haven't reached the tenth generation yet should mean that any info about Gen 11 is far out of the question. That might not be the case though, as recent information seems to touch on exactly what players can expect next.

Over on Reddit, one user shared a post featuring information gained during the infamous Teraleak, which contained thousands of internal files from developer Game Freak. Within that, there were timelines explaining exactly what they were planning to do next (at the time, at the very least), and it could be the most monumental shift we have seen in years.

Specifically, the developer is seemingly planning a new kind of RPG set across all the regions that are based on Japan, namely Kanto, Johto, Hoenn, and Sinnoh. That would be a huge project, and something which fans have been putting together for themselves for a while now, via recompilation projects based on older games.

An official release in that ilk would be huge though, and there is supposedly also a plan to introduce the 11th generation at around the same time, which would make it one of the most fundamentally changing moments in the franchise's history. That could mean a four year cycle for generations is going to become the norm, though Winds and Waves is coming later than expected to make room for the 30th anniversary.

Fans in the responses speculated on what a project that big could look like, with one saying, "It would be interesting to see what sort of story they went with. The criminal organizations include thieves who report to their mafia boss, two extremist groups attempting to terraform the planet, and a nihilistic man who wants to delete the planet entirely. I can’t see any of them working together well."

"Remake of the first 4 regions, in a similar graphics style to black and white, with things like Mega Evolution and modern quality of life features, with a proper battle frontier. I'd love this kind of game," another added.

Whatever does end up happening, we are likely still more than a few years away from seeing it for ourselves, but with Pokémon in a great place right now, it's probably best to just sit back and enjoy it anyway.

Pokémon is a Japanese multimedia franchise created by Satoshi Tajiri and Ken Sugimori, launched by Nintendo, Game Freak, and Creatures in 1996. Centered on fictional creatures called Pokémon, the series spans video games, trading cards, animation, films, merchandise, and competitive events. Players assume the role of Trainers who capture, battle, and trade Pokémon. It is one of the highest-grossing entertainment franchises in history.
