#3350. Prime Video's 'The Mummy' Replacement 'Masters of the Universe' Is Officially a Streaming Hit

Jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

Moviegoers eagerly awaiting the return of The Mummy franchise with next year's The Mummy: Book of the Dead can tide themselves over with another fun action-adventure with heart: the streaming smash hit Masters of the Universe. Based on the iconic 1980s Mattel toy line and Filmation animated series, Masters of the Universe wasn't a box office success, but it's finding a much bigger audience on streaming, topping the Nielsen streaming charts after its Prime Video debut. Fans who love high-octane action-adventure stories that are still full of humor, emotion, and genuine stakes, in the vein of The Mummy, will definitely want to check out Masters of the Universe.

What was interesting about The Mummy was how it veered away from the horror genre of its source material, the original 1932 movie. Instead, the 1999 reboot adopted more of an action-adventure, vintage serial movie style, evoking Steven Spielberg's Indiana Jones movies, with the addition of a slightly more modern vibe and voice within the period setting. That imbued The Mummy reboot with a unique and infectious effervescence that makes it so entertaining to watch.

Masters of the Universe follows a similar playbook: an action-adventure movie that takes itself fairly seriously, but still knows how to have fun and not become overly self-serious. That tone aligns perfectly with the source material, especially considering how silly and goofy the Filmation series could be. Thankfully, director Travis Knight updates the original cartoon's humor, aging it up, resulting in a movie that feels fresh and new, but still speaks to the child in you that loves He-Man and the Masters of the Universe.

Not to mention, Masters of the Universe features incredibly charming leads with Nicholas Galitzine as Adam/He-Man and Camila Mendes as Teela, who showcase wonderful chemistry. Their dynamic evokes the sparks that Brendan Fraser and Rachel Weisz created with their romance in The Mummy as Rick O'Connell and Evelyn Carnahan. The movie presents Adam as a comedically inept young man and HR worker who doesn't look or act like the traditional hero. However, Knight and screenwriter Chris Butler excellently craft Adam with depth as someone who yearns to return to his home planet and must become the legendary He-Man to defend it.

True, Masters of the Universe was born from a 1980s toy line, but therein lies the fun. The movie captures the childlike imagination and whimsy of dumping your action figures in a sandbox and letting your imagination unfold. Part of the joy of the vintage toys was rooted in how they were purposefully designed with their own lore, mythology, and history, providing kids with a jumping-off point to create their own stories within Eternia. Travis Knight, who has already proven he works well with similar material such as the Transformers spin-off Bumblebee, and other fantasy adventures such as Kubo and the Two Strings and Wildwood, truly brings the world of Eternia to life onscreen.

Knight imbues every frame with pure joy, awe, and wonderment, with a visual fidelity to the source material that most adaptations of existing IP and comic book superhero movies lack, right down to the colors of characters' costumes. For fans who grew up with Masters of the Universe, it was an absolute joy to see Eternia, Castle Grayskull, Snake Mountain, and many classic characters brought to vivid life onscreen and faithfully resemble their action figure and animated counterparts. When Adam finally held aloft his magic sword and said the words, "I have the power," becoming He-Man, it was a 10/10 moment with no notes. Plus, the movie is beautifully enhanced by wonderful music composed by Daniel Pemberton, with guitar renditions by rock legend Brian May.

Although Arnold Vosloo is great as Imhotep in The Mummy movies, sometimes the films focused more on cutting-edge visual effects and Imhotep as a CGI monster than creating a genuine threat and epic cinematic villain. But one area where Masters of the Universe outdoes The Mummy is its antagonist: Skeletor (Jared Leto). Make no mistake, Skeletor is the true star of Masters of the Universe, and the new movie excellently realizes the unparalleled overlord of evil with a mix of great practical costume work and digital effects. The CGI enhancement that realizes Skeletor’s bony visage is executed to perfection.

Leto's performance as Skeletor evokes the Filmation series' version, down to the way he constantly derides his minions. However, the new movie still treats Skeletor as a genuine threat despite his maniacal mirth; Leto brings both humorous charisma and genuine menace to Skeletor in a lethal combination. In recent times, it's rare for a major blockbuster to depict a fun villain who unapologetically embraces villainy. So it's great, for once, to have a villain who is evil simply because he enjoys it. Like he says in the movie, "I am the villain. And mmm, does it feel good!"

The Mummy: Book of the Dead will be out in theaters on October 15, 2027. In the meantime, you can check out Masters of the Universe, which is streaming now on Prime Video.

#3349. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the company’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time …

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.)

I’m a big fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”

Apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Yes, Home Depot has already launched its early Black Friday deals, offering deep discounts on major brands of cordless power tools. They also update their sales page on Thanksgiving Day and include Black Friday in-store-only doorbusters as part of their seasonal sales.

For most home tool sets, Ryobi is a solid, durable, and versatile brand. If you plan to use your tools occasionally for home maintenance, this is the best bang for your buck. For daily use or for larger DIY projects, DeWalt tends to be the next best option. These tools have more robust chargers and tend to stand up to more rigorous use than Ryobi tools.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. If you already have a cordless tool set and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something else they can use, a single tool deal might make more sense.

With Apple raising prices across its Mac and iPad lineups in June, citing higher memory chip costs, these sales offer a good opportunity to upgrade without paying full price.

The AirPods Pro 3 are down to $179 from $249, saving you $70 on Apple's latest premium wireless earbuds. They offer improved active noise cancellation over the previous generation, along with redesigned foam-infused ear tips and a heart-rate sensor that tracks workouts without an Apple Watch. They also support Live Translation with a compatible iPhone and carry an IP57 rating for sweat and water resistance. PCMag’s review goes into more detail on how they perform.

The AirPods Max 2, which launched in March, are already down to $449.99 from $549, saving you nearly $100 on Apple's premium over-ear headphones. The biggest upgrade over the original model is the H2 chip, which Apple says makes active noise cancellation up to 1.5 times more effective while introducing features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, and Live Translation. For more on its performance, check out this PCMag review.

The Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS, 42mm) is down to $329 from $399, saving you $70. It covers everything you'd expect from a premium smartwatch, including fitness tracking, health monitoring, notifications, and the ability to take calls when your iPhone is nearby. PCMag gave it an "outstanding" rating in its review and also named it its Gift of the Year for 2026.

If you'd prefer to occasionally leave your iPhone behind, the Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS + Cellular, 42mm) is $70 off, bringing its price down to $429 from $499. It has all the same features as the GPS model but adds cellular connectivity, allowing you to make calls, send messages, and stream music even when your phone isn't nearby (provided you have an active cellular plan).

For a more affordable option, the Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS, 40mm) is down to $199 from $249, saving you $50. It covers the essentials, including workout tracking, daily activity monitoring, and notifications, making it a practical choice if you don't need the Series 12's more advanced health features. Check out PCMag's review for a closer look at what you get for the price.

The Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS + Cellular, 40mm) is also $50 off, bringing its price down to $249 from $299. For an extra $50 over the GPS-only model, you get the convenience of making calls, sending messages, and staying connected without keeping your iPhone nearby, provided you have an active cellular plan. It's worth considering if you regularly go for runs, head to the gym, or step out without your phone but still want to stay reachable.

Apple released the M5 MacBook Air in March with 512GB of base storage, double the previous generation's, along with a faster SSD and an N1 wireless chip that adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Right now, the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air (512GB) is down to $1,249.99 from $1,499. For a closer look at the M5 MacBook Air's performance and features, check out PCMag's review.

If you prefer a more compact laptop but need extra storage, the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with a 1TB SSD is down to $1,399.99 from $1,599, saving you $200. That's twice the storage of the base model, giving you more room for large files, photos, videos, and applications without having to rely as heavily on external drives or cloud storage. You still get the M5 chip, faster SSD performance, and Wi-Fi 7 support, all in a smaller, lighter design.

The M6 Mac mini is down to $949.99 from $1,099, saving you $149 on Apple's latest compact desktop. Its 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU can handle everything from everyday multitasking to photo editing and more demanding creative work, while the upgraded Neural Engine helps with AI-related tasks—Apple says the M6 delivers substantial performance improvements over the earlier M4 model, particularly for graphics and AI workloads. For more on how it performs in everyday use, check out PCMag's review.

The M4 iPad Air launched in March, and the 13-inch model is already down to $949.99 from $1,049, saving you nearly $100. Its M4 chip can comfortably handle demanding tasks like photo editing, digital illustration, and multitasking, while the 13-inch Liquid Retina display gives you plenty of room to work across apps. You also get 256GB of storage for your files and creative projects. For more on what to expect, here's PCMag's review.

If you need more storage for your creative projects, the 13-inch M4 iPad Air with 512GB is $100 off, bringing its price down to $1,149 from $1,249. That's double the storage of the 256GB model, giving you more room for large photo libraries, video projects, downloaded files, and apps without having to rely as heavily on cloud storage.

For those looking for something more powerful, the 11-inch iPad Pro with the M5 chip and 512GB of storage is down to $1,299.99 from $1,399, saving you nearly $100. Along with the faster processor, it offers an Ultra Retina XDR OLED display with ProMotion support for refresh rates up to 120Hz, making it particularly well-suited for creative work, video editing, and other demanding tasks.

The Apple Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad is down to $109 from $129, saving you $20 on a wireless keyboard designed primarily for Mac users. It pairs wirelessly over Bluetooth and can be recharged using USB-C. For a closer look at all that it has to offer, check out PCMag's review.

The Magic Trackpad is down to $130 from $149, taking $19 off an accessory that brings the Multi-Touch gestures and Force Touch pressure sensing of a MacBook trackpad to a desktop setup, across an edge-to-edge glass surface. It connects wirelessly over Bluetooth and has a rechargeable battery that lasts about a month between charges. You can read PCMag's full review to see how it stacks up.

The Apple Pencil Pro is down to $99 from $129, saving you $30 on Apple's most feature-rich stylus. It adds squeeze and barrel-roll gestures, haptic feedback, and Find My support to Apple's stylus lineup, and it pairs and charges magnetically along the side of a compatible iPad, including the M4 iPad Air featured above. The second-generation AirTag, released in January, keeps the original's size so existing holders still fit, while a new Ultra Wideband chip extends Precision Finding range by up to 50% and a redesigned speaker plays 50% louder. Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Among the deals listed here, the M5 MacBook Air with 512 of storage has one of the larger discounts at $249 off, bringing its price down to $1,249.99, from $1499.

If you want more advanced health monitoring and a more premium smartwatch experience, the Series 12 at $329 is worth considering.

#3341. 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

#3340. Shane Gillis' Ex Exposes Alleged Cheating in Scathing Tell-All Essay

Shane Gillis is getting torched by his ex-girlfriend ... who claims the comedian cheated on her for months, leading to an explosive confrontation that left a hole in the wall and a matcha latte flying.

Grace Brassel is spilling all the messy details in a scathing essay for The Cut ... revealing she discovered the alleged infidelity on the Fourth of July last year after borrowing Shane's phone to play music and getting the urge to snoop through his texts.

Grace says she found months of sexually explicit messages between Shane and another woman ... including one in which he admitted he should've slept with her during Super Bowl weekend, when Grace says he'd left her at home.

And that's when the fireworks started ... Grace says she stormed into the living room, demanding to know who the woman was ... but Shane allegedly played dumb and kept fiddling with his Xbox controller as his buddies cleared out.

She admits she completely lost it ... punching a hole in the bathroom wall, throwing her phone and even tossing a chair.

The next morning, Grace claims Shane tried smoothing things over with a matcha latte and a halfhearted apology ... acknowledging the messages were bad and saying he was sorry. She responded by chucking the drink at the wall.

When she demanded to know why he'd cheated, Grace says Shane screamed back that he was insecure, using a homophobic slur to describe himself.

The two began breaking up last August, though Grace says they briefly reconciled before calling it quits for good.

And the cheating allegations are only part of her takedown ... Grace also accuses the comedian of being controlling, emotionally cruel and repeatedly putting her down throughout their relationship.

Gillis told the outlet ... "Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best."

Worth noting ... Grace went on the "For the Girls with Becca Moore" podcast after the split and had plenty of nice things to say about Shane, even saying at the time ... #3339. Apple Calendar got two feature upgrades it really needed in iOS 27

Apple Calendar keeps getting better, including some design updates coming in iOS 27.3. But there are two standout feature upgrades added recently in iOS 27 that Apple’s Calendar app really needed.

I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a new event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

In iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

Apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a big way. Now, you can do things like:

One of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

What are your favorite iOS 27 Apple Calendar upgrades? Let us know in the comments.

#3338. Now These Apple Services Are Down

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector shows user reports of issues across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially showed far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to users on Downdetector, there are currently outages or interruptions to the following Apple services, in order of most to least reported: Apple Support, Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music, Apple Store, Sign In with Apple, Apple Card. As of 1:44 p.m., Apple Support had the most reports, with over 13,000 user complaints. Comments suggest that users cannot log into their iCloud accounts, Apple Accounts, or activate devices, among other issues.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple says that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is currently unavailable. The company's System Status page shows an "issue" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

It's not clear what's causing the issues with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.

Fortunately, with Amazon’s early Black Friday sale, you can get one of its bestsellers, the 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED, for 44% off at $249.99 (originally $449.99).

The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class, lasting up to 18 days (even longer when you’re not using it regularly), which reduces the need for weekly charging, a must for those going off-grid. #3332. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

#3329. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3328. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3325. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3323. Man Plunges to Death at Celebrity-Filled Sierra Towers

A man plunged to his death Tuesday during a condo showing at West Hollywood's famed Sierra Towers ... TMZ has learned.

We're by sources familiar with the situation ... the man first toured an 18th-floor condo, at the same building where the likes of Lindsay Lohan, Cher, Elton John and Courteney Cox have lived, on Monday and told agents he liked the unit enough to come back the next day.

Our sources say the two agents met him there Tuesday and waited while he looked around ... when he didn't return a few minutes later, the agents went looking for him -- and soon realized his body was down on the street.

A source with direct knowledge of the situation tells TMZ ... deputies responded to the swanky high-rise Tuesday afternoon after receiving word a man fell to his death. It is unclear whether the man fell accidentally or jumped on purpose.

Six years earlier, another man died at Sierra Towers during a condo showing. In November 2020, he arranged to see a vacant 27th-floor unit and died after going over the balcony, WEHOonline reported at the time.

The building has been drawing big names for decades. Sandra Bullock owned two condos there, Adam Sandler has owned a unit, and Katy Perry bought an $11 million penthouse in 2023.

#3320. iOS 27 has clever new Messages feature I’ve been using a lot

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#3318. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3317. HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

In the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

It’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

Lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

There were also videos of a woman being detained and carried out by agents as she cried out, sobbed, and, at one point, stated, “We have a work permit!”
